inline.s: Zhang Qing served as a prison officer and bore himself with compassion and caution, every day sweeping and washing the prison with his own hands, and all the more diligently in the heat. He often admonished the jailers, saying: “When a man falls into the net of the law, how could it ever be by his own choosing? We who hold the office of prison officer — if we do not know pity, where are the guilty to go with their pleas?” Food and drink, broth and medicine, and bedding he always had made fine and clean. He loved to read the Lotus Sutra, and whenever a prisoner was executed he would keep a vegetarian fast and recite sutras for him. If a prisoner was innocent, he would always plead on his behalf. He once spoke kindly to the prisoners, asking them: if they were truly guilty, they should admit it themselves, and not falsely implicate the good and upright, thereby deepening their own offense. Later he reached the age of eighty-two and died without illness, and his six sons all became eminent. Seeing this, who will say that the gates of office are not to be entered?

Chen Yuan of the Song was a man of Jintan. In the eighth year of the Xining era the starved dead were beyond counting, and he made pits for ten thousand men; in each pit he set a bowl of rice, a mat, and four sheets of paper, and the corpses he laid away were past reckoning. Afterward his descendants entered official service. Now when human remains lie unburied and exposed to the weather year after year, this is why the aggrieved ghosts whimper and weep by night; how we long for men of benevolence to bury them wherever they are found. In the Chongning era of the Song, an edict went out to the prefectures and counties to choose high, open, barren ground and establish public burial grounds: all the ownerless caskets deposited at monasteries, together with exposed bones and remains, were to be gathered and buried, registers and maps kept for each, markers set up, and houses built as places of offering and libation where kin were permitted to make sacrifice — and this was written into law. Such work was also carried out in the Hongwu era, and I now urge those in authority, and the gentry and common people as well, to promote it as circumstance allows, setting aside land to gather in exposed coffins and bare bones. No merit is greater than this.

Ning Congli was by nature fond of doing good. Pitying those who had no shroud for burial, he often had coffins made and gave them away, and to those who could not afford burial he gave money. He lived to a hundred and died, and appeared in a dream to his family, saying: “In life I built houses and gave them to others; therefore blessing flows down to my descendants, and their success in the examinations shall not fail.” In the end it was so. When a corpse is left unburied it is the most pitiable of things; to give a coffin and lay it to rest wins the deep gratitude of the dark ghosts, and no benevolence is greater. Yet for one of slender means it is hard to keep it up, and it is better to gather a society, dividing it into several branches with a few members in each — for every coffin given, where the society is large each member need put out only a small share, and where it is small each need give no more than a few hundred coppers. It is easily done, and in one district the misery of exposure is at an end. This depends on those who take the work in hand, on their sincerity and diligence. Should there be households of standing, they above all ought to devise every accommodation and make all complete. As for the giving of coffins, one must verify each report as it comes, and must not fail to think out good methods.

Cheng Yide had only a rough grasp of the meaning of characters, yet he labored earnestly to make others do good, and every fine saying and maxim he would have printed to exhort people. One night he dreamed that Lord Wenchang said to him: “You have good thoughts; all your printings have already been reported to the celestial court.” Afterward many of his descendants passed the examinations. Alas, when a man brings forth a good vow, it is heard in Heaven with a sound like thunder; all Buddhas unfailingly protect and remember him, and all the Perfected above unfailingly accord with his heart. These Buddhas and Perfected have long dwelt in liberation, and still they delight in goodness so; how much more should we, in this sea of suffering in the world of men, strive with all our strength to delight in goodness.

Ouyang Xiu of the Song, while serving in the Hanlin Academy, always carried with him several dozen blank visiting cards. Whenever he met a worthy scholar or official who spoke in praise of another’s goodness, he would ask where that man lived, fill in the card, and go to visit him; and if the man proved to be all that had been said, he would spread his good name abroad.

Pang Tong of the Later Han, when he praised men’s goodness, always went beyond the truth, and when people wondered and asked him why, he answered: “These days good men are few and wicked men many. If one wishes to raise up morals and advance the work of the Way, then unless one speaks in fair praise, those who would do good will be few indeed. If I praise ten and miss five, I still gain the half, and I let those of aspiration spur themselves on — is that not permissible?” Lord Guan’s instruction says: “May Heaven ever bring forth good men; may men ever do good deeds; may the mouth ever speak good words.” Master Pang may be called one who well embodied this instruction and who brought increase to the morals of his age.

When Du Zhengxian heard of another’s goodness he rejoiced as though it were his own; when Liu Jixian heard of another’s goodness he praised it without cease; and when Han Zhongxian heard of even a small good deed he would always say: “This is what Qi cannot match.” These gentlemen were public-spirited and loyal, taking thought for the realm, and in gathering up goodness they feared only that they might let some of it slip; that is why they took such delight in commending it. For to recommend the worthy is to benefit the realm and its people — something those in office ought to understand; how could it be mere delight in praising?

When men are in urgent need — in sickness, then doctors and medicine are urgent; in death, then burial rites are urgent; in hunger and cold, then food and clothing are urgent; in debt, then the pressing of creditors is urgent. Their kinds are past counting, and in each case one should help as his means allow and by whatever expedient he can. At such a time one must go forward bravely and without hesitation; otherwise it is a pity to let the opportunity of blessing slip by. Peril is the juncture where life passes over into death — as when a boat capsizes, when fire breaks out, when a family is ruined and lives are lost, down to imprisonment and lawsuits and being brought low by the scheming of others. Emperor Yuan said: “When a man is in hardship and adversity, if one skillfully uses a single word to rescue him, above it aids his ancestors and below it shelters his children and grandchildren.” He also said: “The hand that pushes a man down and the hand that lifts a man up are the same hand; the mouth that ruins a man and the mouth that praises him are the same mouth. Better to be a hand that lifts than a mouth that ruins.” If one can follow these words, his future will of itself be enduring.

The Record of Guiding to Good Fortune says: “When a common man cherishes a heart that loves living beings, he will surely bring relief to others. To save a life costs very little; it is only that those who have food and clothing enough do not know the bitterness of hunger and cold, and so look on such things as dispensable and set them aside lightly. A sallow, starving face does not move them at the moment, and when they see someone lying sick by the roadside they think him past hope and beyond recovery, and so sit by and watch him die. Even those who pass by with a heart of feeling can only sigh; others turn a sidelong eye on him and drive him away. They do not understand that sickness comes of hunger, and that a sick man cannot beg, so that his hunger grows ever deeper; yet it takes no more than three or four pints of grain, carefully tended, for him to be able to go about and beg within a few days, and then he has a chance at life. Or, better still, to save him early, while his face is sallow and he is not yet sick. What a rich man spends on a single night’s lodging is enough to save ten men; what is spent on one rite of a shaman is enough to save a hundred lives. Of a man worth a thousand pieces of gold, let him give one part in ten; of his year’s clothing and food, let him stint one part in ten — that is enough to save a thousand lives. It is very easily done. If several men together raise such a society, set up an empty house, and pile straw matting within it to shelter the poor and the sick, so that they are spared the misery of eating in the wind and sleeping in the wet, then their recovery is all the easier, and in cold weather it is all the more urgent. It is only needful to find good men to manage it. With such a place at each of the four gates, few will die young; extend it until there is one everywhere, and the ghosts of strangers will become rare indeed. For when a man is sick and has no one to care for him, his sickness increases by one; when he is exposed to wind and weather, it increases by a second; when he is destitute and anxious, it increases by a third; and when to this are added hunger in the belly and filth on his clothes, dragged about and shifting from place to place, what hope has he of living again? Try to put yourself in his place — how would such sickness feel? Why begrudge a single grain from the great granary, and not bestow it here? And after all, we are all men alike: had we been born in the wrong place, we should be in just such a state. We are fortunate enough to have sufficiency, and then we wish to enjoy rich feasts and abundance and to secure lasting prosperity for our descendants, while before our eyes men might be saved and we will not part with a single coin. We do not know that flood and fire, robbers and thieves, sickness and sudden calamity can all bring our family fortunes to nothing in an instant, and that our small share of blessing is likewise sheltered by Heaven and Earth — how could a mere miser’s itch for hoarding bring it about? Once impermanence comes, it serves only as funds for our descendants’ wine, lust, gambling, and dissipation, and there are those who will scatter at a single throw what would have been enough to save a thousand lives. How much better to accumulate hidden virtue and seek protection from Heaven — that is the greater course. This principle is perfectly clear; it is only that the stench of copper has stained their bodies, and they simply never think it through.”

Xu Shuwei of the Song once prayed for success in the examinations, and dreamed that a spirit said to him: “If you wish to pass, you must rely on hidden virtue.” Xu reflected that his family was poor and he had no means, and that only medicine would serve; so he studied the medical books with all his mind, and in time mastered their subtleties. He hurried to treat high and low alike, and saved very many lives; his fame grew greater and his good heart more earnest, and afterward he passed the examinations. Now, to save men from sickness is indeed a good cause, but what is one to do when the art of medicine is hard to master? For one of aspiration, devoutly compounding pills, powders, ointments, and elixirs and giving them away, or printing and circulating proven and wondrous prescriptions, is also a method.

Wang Zeng of the Song, on his way to the examinations in the capital, heard on the road the bitter weeping of a mother and daughter. Asking their neighbor, he learned: “They owe money to the government and cannot repay it, and the daughter is to be sold — that is why they weep.” Zeng then sought out their home and questioned them, and finding it was no different, said: “You may sell your daughter to me; as I come and go in office, you may see her from time to time.” He then gave them the amount of their debt and agreed to take the girl in three days. When the time passed and he did not come, the mother sought out the lodging house where Zeng had stayed, and found that he had left a letter directing that the girl be given in marriage to a good man, and that he had already been gone several days. Afterward Zeng came first in all three examinations, and was enfeoffed as Duke of Yi.

Wu Kui of the Song was a close friend of Wang Pengnian. When Wang died, his family was too poor to bury him; Kui had his eldest son see to the funeral rites and bury him, relieved the needs of his household, and arranged the marriages of his two daughters. Afterward he rose to the office of chancellor and was given the posthumous title Wensu.

Xie Kai of the Ming was a man of wealth. Whenever relatives or old friends lacked the means for a wedding or a funeral he would always relieve them, and when anyone came to him in urgent need he would go to their aid through scalding water and fire. He once said: “Who does not wish to amass much? But wealth is the storehouse of resentment. I know only to plant goodness, which may be bequeathed to my descendants — what leisure have I for gold and jade?” His son Lun served as an imperial censor and rose to the office of Grand Secretary.

In Xinjian there was a great famine. A man reduced to the utmost extremity had about a pint of rice left, so he cooked it and put poison in it, intending that he and his wife should eat their fill together and die. Just then the village headman came to collect the silver due for the poll tax; seeing the rice, he was about to eat it, and the poor man hastily stopped him, saying: “That is not for you to eat,” and weeping, told him why. The headman was moved to pity and said: “Why go to such lengths so suddenly? My house is poor, but I still have five pecks of millet; come with me and carry it home, and you may hold out a little longer.” The poor man carried the millet home and found fifty pieces of gold inside it. He reflected: “This must be government silver,” and hurried to return it. The headman said: “It is not government silver at all — it must be a gift from Heaven.” So they divided it equally, and both passed the year in comfort.

Sun Jue of the Song was prefect of Fuzhou, where great numbers of people were imprisoned for debts owed to the government. It happened that a rich man offered five million coins, asking to repair a Buddha hall. Jue said: “You give your money wishing to obtain blessing. The Buddha hall is not badly decayed; how much better to use the money to pay the prisoners’ debts to the government, so that several hundred men are released from the misery of the cangue and chains. Then even the Buddha and the patriarchs would smile and let down their compassion — would not the blessing obtained be greater?” The rich man accordingly paid the money to the government, and the prisons were emptied. His descendants became eminent and honored, and Jue rose in office to the rank of Pillar of State.

The cases above are all of relieving men in the extremities of burial, sickness, marriage, debt, separation, and poverty, and the abundance of Heaven’s recompense in each was exceedingly swift. Alas, men’s urgent troubles occur wherever one turns; those with means who meet with them ought indeed to relieve them well, and those without means should also devise clever expedients, doing all that their heart and strength can according to circumstance. As for a poor harvest and a hungry people, this is foremost and greatest among all urgent needs. If those in office and those of wealth did not bring forth the surplus of human effort to make up the deficiency of Heaven’s course, relieving and aiding them, could the poor escape dying in the ditches? I have touched on this thought before in my annotations on loyalty, but did not develop it fully; therefore now, after discussing the relief of the various urgent needs, I speak of it once more and at length. It is my wish only that benevolent men in authority and good-hearted gentry and common folk alike may thoroughly take it to heart.

Fan Chunren of the Song was prefect of Qingzhou. In a year of famine the starved dead filled the roads, and Chunren asked to release the grain of the ever-normal granaries to relieve them. The officials of the commandery said that a memorial must first be sent. Chunren said: “If men do not eat, they die. If we memorialize first and release it afterward, how can it arrive in time? Let none of you worry; if there is any guilt, I shall bear it myself.” So he released the grain that very day, and those he saved were beyond counting. Afterward he rose in office to Academician, was enfeoffed as Duke of Gaoping, and given the posthumous title Zhongxuan.

Zhao Bian of the Song was prefect of Yuezhou. In a great drought throughout Wu and Yue, before the people had yet begun to starve he wrote out inquiries to the counties under him: how many places were stricken; how many country people would need relief from the granaries; how many sites of dikes and ditches could be built by hiring the people to labor; how much of the money in the treasury and grain in the granaries could be released; how many rich households could be enlisted to contribute grain. All this he recorded one by one in the registers. He then enrolled the orphaned, the aged, and the sick who could not feed themselves — more than twenty-one thousand nine hundred souls. He examined the old precedents: in a year of relief for the poor, the grain given out was to stop at three thousand piculs. Bian selected what the rich households contributed, together with other surpluses, and obtained more than forty-eight thousand piculs of grain to supplement the expense. From the first day of the tenth month each person received one pint of grain a day, children half of that. Fearing that the crowds would mingle indiscriminately, he had men and women come on different days, and each person received two days’ food at once. Fearing that they would drift away as refugees, he established fifty-seven places in the cities and the countryside for giving out grain, so that each might receive it conveniently, and he announced that those who left their homes would be given nothing. Reckoning that the officials would not suffice, he took clerks who held no office but dwelt within the borders, gave them food, and entrusted them with duties. He told the rich that they must not close their stores, and whereas every other prefecture posted a ban on the price of rice, Bian ordered that those who had rice might sell it at a raised price as they wished. He himself untied his gold belt and laid it in the courtyard, commanding that rice be bought with it, and from this the givers gathered like clouds. He further released fifty-two thousand piculs of government grain and sold it at a level price for the people’s convenience, establishing eighteen places for the purchase of grain, so that buyers need not rush about. He also hired the people to repair the city walls — four thousand one hundred men, performing thirty-eight thousand days of labor — and reckoned their wages in grain at twice the rate. When the people took loans at interest, he told the rich to lend freely and wait for the harvest, the government undertaking to press for repayment. Children abandoned by their parents he had taken in and raised by every means. In the spring of the following year sickness spread among the people; he set up infirmaries for the sick who had no home, and enlisted two monks, charging them to see to medicine, food, and drink, so that nothing should be missed at the proper time. All who died he had gathered and buried where they lay. By law, relief for the poor was to end after the third month; that year it continued until the fifth. When matters required a memorial, he acted on whatever was expedient and carried it out, Bian taking it all upon himself and not burdening his subordinates. Morning and night he exhausted heart and strength, and in nothing, great or small, did he fail to act in person. At that time, in drought and pestilence, the people of other commanderies died by nearly half, but in the region Bian tended, none were left unprovided for. He afterward served as chancellor to Emperor Shenzong and was a famous minister of the Song.

Fu Bi of the Song served as vice commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, and when someone falsely accused him of wishing to ally with the Khitan and raise troops, Emperor Renzong was angry and demoted him to be prefect of Qingzhou. At that time there was a great flood north of the Yellow River, and starving people flowed into his territory with no food and nothing to do but await death. The duke raised more than a hundred thousand bushels of grain, storing and distributing it wherever he went; he also requisitioned more than a hundred thousand rooms, public and private, that stood idle, and dispersed the people among them; medicine and doctors were all provided. The wealth of the mountains and marshes he let the refugees take, and their owners were not permitted to forbid it. Those who died he buried in great common graves, and those who followed him came as to a market. Someone said to Bi that this was no way to conduct oneself amid danger and suspicion, and that calamity was beyond foreseeing. Bi said: “Would I trade my single body for the lives of six or seven hundred thousand people?” He carried it out with ever greater force. The next year the wheat ripened abundantly; he calculated the distances each had come, gave them grain, and sent them home. Those who lived numbered more than five hundred thousand. When the emperor heard of it he sent envoys to commend him and appointed him vice minister of rites; afterward he became chancellor, was enfeoffed as Duke of Zheng, lived to eighty, and was given the posthumous title Wenzhong and a place in the ancestral temple.

Ding Qinghui, Duke Bin, of the Ming, was a man of Jiashan. He delighted in goodness without wearying, and took especial pains for famine relief. In the dinghai year of the Wanli era there was a great flood and the price of rice soared; the duke first had his household exchange rice for cloth at the current value, adding four pints of rice to each bolt, which cost him more than a thousand piculs of stored grain. He also built up the embankments of the fields to guard against drought and flood, giving out rice by the yard of work, at a cost of six hundred and fifty piculs of his stores. The next year the famine grew worse; the duke set up gruel yards, where those who came to eat numbered several thousand a day. He also sought out the aged and weak who could not come and gave to them separately, and this continued until the ninetieth day. In autumn there was again cruel drought, and the duke relieved the starving people by the waterside, all his plans being good measures for famine relief, and very many were kept alive. In the winter months the victims of the disaster suffered much from the cold; the duke sought out everywhere those who were alone and bare, enrolled them in registers, and gave them tickets, to come and receive their share at the appointed time. He brought out all the cloth he had earlier exchanged, added cotton to it, and gave each person two bolts of cloth and four catties of cotton. Reckoning the whole, he distributed more than twelve thousand four hundred piculs of rice, thirty-four thousand bolts of cloth, and sixty thousand and eighty catties of cotton. In the wushen year there was another great flood; the duke had the censorate and the provincial authorities memorialize for relief loans, and sent orders to Wu and Chu that no one was to block the grain trade; government silver was released and transported by four routes, and he further donated his own funds for broad relief. In the jiazi year there was incessant rain, and the duke again opened the granaries to give relief, distributing three thousand piculs of rice — four relief efforts in all. The duke also reckoned that the small households of the whole county who held only two or three mu of land owed about three thousand taels of silver in tax, and he paid it all on their behalf. At ninety the court sent greetings and built him a memorial arch; he lived nearly a hundred years.

Zheng Gangzhong of the Song was a man of Jinhua and served as assistant prefect of Wenzhou. In a year of famine he brought out his salary and urged the sale of grain, and the prefect said: “I fear the real benefit will not reach the starving.” He answered: “That is not difficult.” He then took ten thousand coins and stamped a character on each, and going out again into the lanes and alleys, gave one coin to each starving person he met, warning them: “Do not wipe off the stamped character. Tomorrow you will receive rice in exchange for the coin.” Not one of the starving was missed. Of all methods of distributing grain, none is better than this. There is also the proposal, in relieving famine, to give food by the head, issued once every half month; the people are then spared the labor of running about and can stay at home and work, while we are spared hired labor and miscellaneous costs, and more lives can be saved — and it also prevents embezzlement. Someone said: “Giving food by the head would surely be abused by false claimants, and cannot be carried out.” He replied: “There is a way to arrange it. First distribute gruel for three or five days, keeping men and women apart, and allow them to bring bottles, to take home for the old and the young. Give each person a tally. Record the surnames of each village’s people, gather them in one place, and forbid them to scatter — thus you may reckon the number of a village. Then go to the villages in person to investigate, distinguishing the moderately poor from the very poor; better to let one pass than to take one in wrongly. Agree that they shall come with bags to receive their grain and go home. For the aged, the weak, and widows who cannot carry a load, convert it at the current price into coin, giving a little more rather than less.” This too is a most fitting plan; it is only for the benevolent, according to the time, to adapt and arrange it as is convenient.

Zhu Ran of Yanping, whenever there was a poor harvest, set up gruel to give great relief to the starving. On the day of his son’s provincial examination, a neighbor dreamed that a man came galloping with news that he was the top graduate, holding a great banner on which were four characters: “The recompense of giving gruel.” And indeed he passed in quick succession and stood first in the realm. Men of old, in discussing methods of relief, held the setting up of gruel to be the lowest; yet when Xi Wenxiang relieved the great famine in Jiangnan he especially advocated gruel relief, saying that in distributing silver and rice one must compile and verify the rolls in exact detail and cut off every abuse, while the lives of the starving hang by a thread — how can they be kept waiting? With gruel, all who are relieved are genuinely poor, and it is the most urgent measure for relieving hunger. From this one sees that even the lowest method has its proper time for use; it lies with the man on the spot to weigh the circumstances and judge what is fitting — it cannot be bound by a single rule. Some hold that setting up a yard to distribute gruel, though a fine thing, is not in fact wholly good: for one thing, the aged and weak cannot come; again, those several li away must bear hunger and brave wind and cold and easily fall ill; and if they come ten li and return ten li, then wait in a crowd and press forward, they cannot all be served at once. If they eat much their bellies swell, and if they eat little they are hungry again. Moreover, the noisome vapors steam upward, and unexpected calamities often arise there: some die on the spot after eating the gruel, and some, at a single stoop, bring the gruel spurting back out. To speak of it is heartrending. This should be understood, and then one sees the truth of doing good. Now a better method has been found: nothing is so good as the gruel carrying-pole. For each load, five or six pints of white rice are boiled into gruel and kept in a covered bucket with a little fire beneath to keep it from going cold, while outside is a small basket holding ten bowls, ten pairs of chopsticks, and a little salted vegetable. The pole is carried to the great thoroughfares or beyond the city walls, and when the poor are met they are made to sit in rows; when one meal has been given, water is borrowed to wash the vessels, so that they may serve those who come after. It is reckoned that each load can feed forty or fifty people, and ten loads suffice to feed four or five hundred. Thus one may go lane by lane and alley by alley, holding them each day, and truly there is the substance of relieving people at any hour, without the abuses of a yard that gathers crowds together. This is the most convenient and most fitting method of gruel relief.

Wei Shiju loved to give. When the harvest failed and rice grew dear, he would open his granaries and sell grain at a level price, taking only half the current price. He once said: “Half the price in a bad year is the full price in a good year; though one takes less, it is no loss.” He constantly relieved the poverty of his relatives and friends, and the whole commandery depended on him for relief. His son Shoujie served as a minister.

Huang Chengshi of the Song, at every harvest, would put out money to buy rice, and when the next year came and the old grain was exhausted before the new was in, he would sell it to the common people without raising the price, giving the same measure as before. Afterward he dreamed that the Perfected Lord of the Purple Palace said to him: “I grant you a son who shall rise to the office of minister, and you yourself shall be entered in the registers of the immortals.” In the end both proved true. The Perfected Qiu Changchun of the Yuan said: “Selling rice at a level price is the first and greatest expedient; truly it is immeasurable merit to relieve men in a year of famine. Let him who has means buy up grain widely at harvest, or if he has fields, store up what he gathers himself, and when scarcity comes sell it out at the original price. To himself there is no loss, to others the greatest benefit — why should he not delight in doing it? Next best is to reduce the current price somewhat; selling evenly is still better.”

Deng Chengmei gathered his clansmen to form a Society for Universal Benefit, taking as its meaning that a bad year should not be able to kill them. The method was this: in a good harvest each mu contributed one or two pecks of grain; in the following spring it was lent out at two parts in ten interest, and repaid at the autumn threshing floor. Chengmei managed the affair with strict fairness. Afterward, when drought and famine came, he not only saved his neighbors and clansmen but was able to reach others as well. He lived to the age of seventy-five, and on the day he died a rare fragrance filled the room; the neighbors saw countless underworld servitors, who declared that they had come to welcome a certain city god.

Cao Shimei was poor but loved goodness, and a monk taught him that to earnestly exhort others and help others could also create merit. From then on Shimei gathered people to form good societies of every kind — distributing gruel, giving clothing, giving medicine, giving ginger broth, releasing living creatures, cherishing written words, giving coffins, burying the unburied, repairing bridges and roads, and the like. Others contributed money and he contributed labor, and so it went every year, with ever greater force the longer it lasted; in famine years he was especially earnest in urging relief. Afterward he traded in oil with a rich family and gradually gained more than five thousand pieces of gold, and his children and grandchildren enjoyed ample blessing in peace. In all things the rich find merit easy and the poor find it hard; yet to stand in a place where effort is difficult and still be able to strive — this is what sets such a man apart from others. The ancients said: “When a poor man performs a hundred deeds of merit, it counts as a thousand performed by the rich and honored.” Seen in this light, how can the poor man abandon himself and fail to cultivate a resolute heart and bitter determination?

Duan Ershiba had stored up grain in several dozen granaries, and when the year of famine came he wanted to demand a high price. The government sent an envoy to borrow grain for relief, and he agreed; but the next morning, seeing the starving gathered and waiting, he regretted it and would not give out the grain. As the crowd began to clamor, he and his household shut the doors and refused the people. Suddenly there came a great wind and rain, which scattered his grain into the streets, gathered in heaps each by its own color, and the starving struggled to take it. Duan was struck dead by lightning.

Looking through the records of humane and cruel deeds in years of famine and of the recompense of calamity and blessing, the entries are so numerous that they cannot all be set down; it is not meant that they end here. The earlier Confucians said: “Famine is a matter of fate, yet the heart of Heaven is benevolent and loving, and its compassion for the starving multitudes is doubly deep.” Therefore the wise accord with Heaven and bring down auspiciousness, while the foolish defy Heaven and bring down punishment — this is a necessary principle. The recompense of calamity takes many forms, and it comes more swiftly than the recompense of blessing. Not only does the crime of closing one’s stores draw the stroke of Heaven; even he who hoards gold in miserliness and coldly watches a dying man without saving him hardens his heart and injures principle, and his condemnation is all the heavier. As for one who dwells deep in a fine house, who does not hear the cry of hunger, who does not see the gaunt bodies in the ditches, or who wishes to save them yet hesitates and delays and does not perceive how many have already starved to death — he too turns his back on the heart of Heaven, and guilt is not escaped. But if one is a father and mother to the people and is indifferent, taking no concern for their suffering, procrastinating and letting matters go astray, or if one is a clerk who breeds abuses and practices wickedness so that the people never taste the real benefit — such a one’s crime will not be escaped even through ten thousand kalpas. The ancients said: “To save one life extends one’s years by a full cycle.” How much more for a man of power and position, who with a single raising of his hand may save a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand lives. Therefore one in authority is as though in a mountain of treasures, free to gather what he will — let him beware of returning empty-handed. The most precious course is to be the first to take the lead and imitate the great relief of the ancients; and even he whose means are limited should gather men of truly good heart, urge and collect contributions far and wide, and carry it out as circumstance allows. Then perhaps the ditches may be turned into mats of comfort, and hidden merit will be vast, and the recompense of Heaven will not fail. That this is spoken of so fully in these pages comes of painstaking thought and deep intent, the most earnest of admonitions. And let it be enjoined: should a famine come and relief be needed, let these sayings and cases on famine relief be quickly gathered and polished, printed to spread the exhortation, and widely sent to the stricken cities and countryside, for gentry and common folk and wealthy households to read closely, and posted plentifully in busy places — this is truly great goodness, bringing boundless blessing.

Appendix: Chen Pengnian of the Suzhou prefecture in the Qing, with annotations on the twenty measures for famine relief. In the forty-seventh year of the Kangxi era, flood and drought followed one upon the other, and Lord Chen submitted these measures with a request that the governors and military commanders of Jiangsu and Zhejiang promulgate and carry them out. At first rice was twenty coppers a pint; in less than two months it could be bought for only eight or nine coppers a pint, and the people sang that they had been born again. 1. Prohibit the making of wine from glutinous rice. 2. Prohibit the distilling of liquor from wheat. 3. Prohibit the pressing of oil from yellow beans. 4. Prohibit the making of sugar from coarse and polished broken rice. 5. Prohibit the making of gluten from bran. Annotation: order that it be sold at once to the poor, to make cakes and pass the famine. With these five strict prohibitions, a middling county saved several hundred piculs of rice a day and more, so that the price of rice was seen to fall daily. 6. Prohibit butchering and the sale of cooked food. Annotation: to save wealth and cherish blessing; only the sale of rice-flour foods, wheaten foods, and vegetarian foods is permitted. 7. Urge the great houses and rich merchants to contribute rice for famine relief. Annotation: that year Lord Dong Tianjuan of Pinghu county, instructed by Lord Chen, first had twenty plaques reading “Rich but Unkind” made and piled up in the county hall, then went in person to the rich households to urge contributions. His utter sincerity moved them, and he used both hardness and softness in turn. He went first to the villages, and meeting three stubborn rich families, nailed the plaques to their gates and permitted accusations to be lodged against them; and in every case of land judged for redemption or increase their family property was cut by half. From this, from the villages to the city, many gave gladly. Besides giving rice and money, he set up yards everywhere to distribute gruel, and also gave medicine, relieving them for several months until the new grain was eaten. When the contributions proved more than was needed, the surplus was apportioned back to the rich households, and the lives saved were beyond counting. Zhen Dexiu, Master Xishan of the Song, said: “To bestow kindness and relief on the poor will surely obtain the protection of Heaven and Earth.” This is spoken from principle. If one speaks in terms of advantage and harm: where there are no starving people there are no robbers, and where there are no robbers the villages are at peace — this too is to the advantage of the rich. Chen Jiting said: “For famine relief, the gentry and rich households of each district and each village must each relieve the poor near them, and then of itself the whole county will have no one starved.” Huang Zhen said: “Famine relief lies wholly in urging division — urging the rich households to bestow kindness on the poor, giving from their surplus to make up the deficiency. This is the way of Heaven and the law of the state. If a man thinks only of being rich alone and does not consider the miserable straits of famine, then even should he by good fortune escape the law of the state, he will surely not escape the punishment of Heaven.” I have also heard Master Zhu say: “In urging division to relieve the people’s urgent need, one cannot but bear a little; if one calculates too deeply on behalf of the rich, I fear nothing will ever be carried out. Severity overcoming tenderness is what brings the matter through.” Thus Lord Chen deeply grasped Master Zhu’s way of famine relief. 8. Undertake public works to relieve want. Annotation: such as building city walls, opening canals, and repairing bridges and roads, so that craftsmen may get food. 9. Relax the prohibitions on mountains and marshes. Annotation: such as exempting miscellaneous grains from harsh taxes to facilitate water transport, and not forbidding the gathering of firewood, so that people may have something to fill their mouths and not drift into becoming robbers. 10. For those whose crimes admit of pity or doubt, allow them to redeem their offenses with grain, which is taken for famine relief. 11. Regardless of whether they be officials, soldiers, commoners, women, monks, or Daoists — persons of every kind who can assist in relief: for small amounts, give them a plaque and a reward; for large amounts, report to the higher authorities and await the imperial decree. 12. Invite famous physicians and open dispensaries to save the sick. 13. Teach the people near the mountains to gather pine and cypress to relieve hunger. Annotation: the Records of Broad Learning says that in a famine year, when there is no food to be had, one may finely pound the juice of pine and cypress and take it with water, until hunger ceases; taken with thin rice gruel it is even better. Each dose uses five measures of pine juice and three of cypress juice, ground and taken; or one may use pine needles alone. But one must abstain from all other food, and of itself it will relieve hunger and ward off sickness. 14. Mitigate punishments. Annotation: in a bad year many break the law, so deal with them leniently. 15. Economize on ceremonies. Annotation: for capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice, reduce the ceremonial forms. 16. Lend the people seed grain. Annotation: lest the land’s fertility be wasted. 17. Take strict precautions against robbers. Annotation: lest they harm the people. 18. Officials, gentry, and village elders should, on the first and fifteenth of each month, observe fasts, bathe, take up incense, and walk on foot to pray in the various temples, beseeching blessings for the people. Annotation: a famine year is brought about by the shared karma of the people; prayer and repentance can turn back the great decree, and this too is one of the famine policies of the Rites of Zhou. 19. In each prefecture and county, choose those of talent and virtue to take charge of famine administration. Annotation: such as managing the giving of rice and the distribution of gruel, so that the common people receive real benefit. When the work is done, report them to the throne together with those who donated silver and rice. 20. Let boats carrying cotton, rice, beans, and wheat pass the customs barriers for one month, and send men to haul and escort them. Annotation: when cotton and rice arrive daily from other prefectures, the price falls daily; this is a great device for turning scarcity into abundance.

The teaching on relieving urgent need has been set out fully above. As for saving men from peril, the principle is much the same, though it feels more closely bound up with life and death. Several cases are appended below.

Zhang Baihu of Gaoyou, from his boat, saw far off a man straddling the back of a capsized vessel, now sinking and now rising above the water, crying out for rescue. Zhang urgently called a fishing boat to go to his aid; the fishermen did not respond, and only set out when he offered them ten taels of silver. When the man was brought in, it was his own son.

Zhou Bida of the Song dynasty, during the Shaoxing era, was overseeing the Hangzhou Pharmaceutical Bureau. A fire broke out within the bureau, and by law the one who let the fire start was to die. The duke said: “If this fire had started from an official source, what punishment would then be fitting?” The clerk said: “Dismissal from office and reduction to commoner status.” The duke said: “Can I, for the sake of my single person, bear to watch more than ten men die?” So he falsely confessed to the crime and was stripped of office, and every family among them survived. Afterward he became prime minister.

Lei Youzhong of the Song dynasty, in his campaign against Wang Jun, wished to massacre the city. At that time the Shu scholars Fan Can and Fan Sui, men who prized integrity and were rich in learning, together with Master Wenjian, renowned for his conduct, went forward in a body to remonstrate. Bowing their heads to the ground, they said: “The men of Shu are good-natured and weak; those who followed him under duress did so only from fear of death. On the day the city falls, we beg that there be no slaughter, and that only the ringleaders of the wicked be cut down.” Youzhong, seeing three men of such generous spirit, forgetful of themselves for the sake of others and speaking from utter sincerity, changed countenance and said: “Had I not heard the words of these elders, I would well-nigh have acted rashly.” And so the whole city was preserved intact. The descendants of the Fan clan became noble and eminent, and Wenjian attained realization of the Way.

A certain Feng rose early in the depth of winter and met on the road a man lying in the snow, his body already half frozen. Feng quickly took off his own cotton garments and clothed him with them, then supported him home and revived him. He dreamed that a spirit said to him: “You have saved a man’s life, and out of utter sincerity. You shall be granted Han Qi as your son.” Later a son was born to him, named Qi, who rose to the greatest eminence.

Wang Zhiren, a merchant of Huizhou, was thirty years old and without a son. On his travels he came upon a woman who, holding her child, was about to throw herself into the water. He stopped her and asked the reason. The woman said: “My husband is poor, and we keep a pig to pay our rent. Yesterday he went out to hire himself to another, and when the buyer of the pig came I sold it, never suspecting that all the silver I received was counterfeit. I fear my husband will beat me when he returns, and there is no way left to keep body and soul together. That is why I would die.” Ren was moved to pity and gave her silver to help her. When her husband learned of it, he suspected she had been deceived, and dragged her to Ren’s lodging to question him. Ren had already gone to bed, and the husband made his wife knock at the door, saying: “I am the woman who tried to drown herself, come to give thanks.” Wang said sternly: “You are a young wife, and I am a lone traveler. How is it fitting for us to meet in the dark of night? If you have anything to say, come with your husband in the morning.” Only then did the husband, startled, say: “My wife and I are both here.” Ren then threw on his clothes and came out to receive them; and no sooner had he opened the door than the wall collapsed, and the bed on which he had lain was crushed to powder. Husband and wife sighed in wonder, gave their thanks, and departed. Afterward Ren had eleven sons and enjoyed a great old age.

Pei Du of the Tang dynasty was visiting the Xiangshan Temple when he picked up two jade belts and one rhinoceros-horn belt. He waited for the owner, but as evening came the man still had not appeared. At dawn he went again, and a woman came weeping, saying: “My father has been imprisoned though innocent. Yesterday I borrowed these precious belts, thinking to ransom him from his crime, but to my misfortune I lost them here. There is now no escape from disaster.” Du, deeply moved, returned them to her. Previously there had been a physiognomist who read Du’s face and declared that he was certain to die of starvation; meeting him again at this later time, he said: “Your countenance has suddenly changed. You must have done hidden virtue that has reached others; your future is beyond anything I can foretell.” Afterward Pei Du was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jin and granted the title Grand Tutor.

The roads of the world are perilous and steep, and the dangers that befall us are of more than one kind. A man of benevolence extends the same care to all such cases, doing in every matter whatever lies within his power; these cannot all be recorded here in full. As for the perils of capital punishment and imprisonment, where death and life hang in the balance — these are graver still than the rest. They are set out below, within the annotation “Taking what is light and making it heavy,” and so are not appended here.

People today, when they see another’s gain or loss, cannot feel it as they would their own gain or loss; it is simply that a whole heart of selfishness is fixed upon themselves, wanting to gain and fearing to lose. So there arises the thought of dreading that another may gain, and of preferring that another should lose. At first it is no more than self-interest, but afterward it gradually turns to harming others. Yet what have envy of another’s success and delight in another’s failure to do with the affairs of men? They only ruin one’s own character and plant evil causes for one’s own destruction. They do not know that the work of sages and worthies is precisely to dissolve the view of a self, and that the insight of a man of understanding must likewise break through vulgar sentiment. If one awakens to the truth that self and other share one source, and that gain and loss are the decree of Heaven, then in seeing another’s gain one will not merely refrain from envy but will support him in a hundred ways; and in seeing another’s loss one will not merely refrain from delight but will rescue and protect him by every means. This is where one’s own true benefit lies.

Lord Di Liang of the Tang dynasty, serving as legal officer and military aide of Bingzhou, found that a certain Mr. Zheng was to be sent as envoy to a far country, though his mother was old and ill. Lord Di said: “His mother is in such a state — how can he be allowed to bear the grief of a journey of ten thousand li?” He went to the chief secretary Lin Renji and asked to go in his place. Renji had long been at odds with the adjutant Li, and because of this he said to him: “Lord Di is like this — can we not feel ashamed of ourselves?” And so they were reconciled.

Xue Yuan served as minister of the state of Yan, yet he could not keep his heart level: he envied others their gains and rejoiced in their losses; he would not recommend worthy men, and moreover envied them, so that they could not advance. One of his sons died in prison, and the rest were crippled. Gongming Zigao gave him the Classic of Central Admonitions, and Yuan repented and vowed to strive in its practice; only one son was preserved.

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty said: As for a man’s response to the realms of wealth, beauty, fame, and profit in this world, let me make it clear by analogy. Suppose there is a fire blazing here, and five things set beside it. The first is dry grass, which catches alight the moment it is touched. The second is wood, which catches alight when blown upon. The third is iron, which cannot be set alight but can be melted. The fourth is water, which not only does not catch alight but can put the fire out; yet if it is poured into a cauldron, it may still be brought to the boil. The fifth is empty space, which lets the flames scorch and burn as they will, its own substance forever as it is, and which need not even be extinguished, for the fire will presently go out of itself. One whose heart is level should contemplate the matter in this way.

As for a man’s shortcomings, they are like the name of one’s father or mother: the ear may hear it, but the mouth may not speak it. And though the mouth indeed may not speak it, that the ear also should not hear it is better still. Broadly speaking, who is without shortcomings? To expose them cannot but spread them abroad, diminishing a man’s good name and undermining his long-held integrity. To whom then should the blame be ascribed? Unless he were a petty man utterly without scruple, no one would do such a thing. As for one’s own strengths, they are like the wealth of a good merchant: deeply stored, it fares well; shallowly displayed, it invites danger. In life a man is sure to have some strength; the point is to conceal it and nurture it, renewing it day by day and again anew, and only then can virtue be perfected. Laozi said: “Great virtue wears the countenance of a fool.” Zisi said: “It shines forth day by day from obscurity.” The teachings of the sages are luminously clear, and a man should examine himself.

In the time of the Zhou dynasty, King Zhuang of Chu was feasting at night with his assembled ministers when the candles went out, and one of the drunken guests pulled at the robe of a concubine. She snatched off his cap tassel and told the king of it. The king said: “I gave the man wine until he was drunk; to expose a woman’s honor because of that is not something I would do.” So he ordered those about him not to relight the lamps, and proclaimed: “Whoever drinks with me tonight and does not break off his tassel has not made merry.” All the ministers broke off their tassels, took their full joy, and departed. Later, when the king did battle with Jin, he saw one man fighting with might and main — it was the one who had broken off his tassel.

Han Qi of the Song dynasty spent long years in the Secretariat, and whenever he came upon documents that attacked men’s hidden faults, he sealed and noted them with his own hand and would not let others see them. Wang Su served as remonstrating official and said: “Men of talent are hard to come by. In times of peace we should cherish them for the court’s sake, and must not pry into men’s private affairs to expose their shortcomings.” Cheng Mingdao, as censor, told his sovereign: “To have me gather up omissions and make good defects, that I can do; but if you would have me search out the merits and faults of your ministers to buy a name for uprightness, that I cannot do.” Xu Wenzhen was entertaining guests when one of them took a gold cup and put it inside his cap. The servants searched for the cup, and the duke said: “It has already been put away.” The man, being drunk, let his cap fall and the cup dropped to the ground; the duke pretended not to know, and slipped it back into the man’s sleeve. Wen Zhengming by nature disliked hearing of others’ faults, and when anyone began to speak of them he deftly turned the talk to another subject. These several lords held fast to honesty and generosity, and it was fitting that they should enjoy great emoluments and be famed ministers.

Tian Ji, relying on his talent, was caustic and cruel: he loved to appraise and censure the shortcomings of the sages and worthies of antiquity and of the well-known men of his own day. After his death, the underworld tribunals, because of this karma, each day sent three snakes and two centipedes in and out of his seven bodily openings, and when a full year had passed he was reborn as a woman. This is what he told his wife in a dream. Zhang Gongchen said: “Do not lightly cast aside another’s good; do not lightly believe another’s words; do not lightly take pleasure in another’s discomfiture; do not lightly speak of another’s shortcomings. All these are ways of holding fast to honesty and generosity, and the exposing of shortcomings in particular is the very root of meanness and treachery. How much more so in the case of Tian Ji, who slandered the sages and worthies besides — how could the underworld’s punishment ever have shown him leniency?”

Ouyang Xiu of the Song dynasty excelled in letters, yet whenever he faced a guest he spoke much of affairs of state and did not touch on letters. Cai Xiang excelled in affairs of state, yet whenever he faced a guest he spoke much of letters and did not touch on affairs of state. Both lords were good at concealing themselves, and yet in the end they enjoyed great renown and both reached the highest eminence.

In the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty, Lu, Luo, Wang, and Yang all enjoyed great renown for their letters, and everyone expected that they would become noble and eminent. Pei Xingjian saw them and said: “For a scholar to go far, he must first have capacity and discernment, and only afterward literary art. Though Bo and the others have letters, they are flighty, restless, and shallow in display — are they vessels fit to enjoy rank and emolument? Master Yang is somewhat more calm and still; if he can but come to a good end, that will be fortunate enough.” In the end it fell out exactly as he said. Indeed, talent and ability are not equal to learning and insight, nor spirit and integrity to the measure of one’s virtue, nor letters to conduct and right action; men of old have already said so plainly. Therefore the display of one’s strengths is a thing a gentleman does not do.

Cui Yuan of the Later Han wrote in his Motto at the Right of the Seat: “Speak not of others’ faults, nor lean upon your own strong points. In giving, beware of keeping count; in receiving, beware of forgetting. The world’s praise is not worth the craving; let benevolence alone be your rule and line. Act only after the heart is stilled; what harm can slander do? Let not your name outrun the truth; to keep one’s folly is what sages prize. Though steeped in black, be not stained; let a dim and hidden light dwell within. The soft and yielding are companions of life; Laozi warned against the hard and strong. The strutting walk is the petty man’s ambition; the vast and distant is therefore hard to measure. Be careful in speech, be temperate in food and drink; to know contentment surpasses all ill fortune. If in this practice you but persevere, in time its fragrance will come of itself.”

Yuan Liaofan of the Ming dynasty, in his Chapter on the Virtue of Humility, says: The Book of Changes states: “The way of Heaven takes from the full and adds to the humble; the way of Earth changes the full and flows toward the humble; ghosts and spirits bring disaster on the full and blessing on the humble; the way of men hates the full and loves the humble.” Thus in the hexagram of Humility all six lines are auspicious. The Book of Documents says: “Fullness invites loss; humility receives benefit.” I have many times sat the examinations together with various gentlemen, and whenever I saw a poor scholar about to succeed, there was always a certain glow of humility about him that one could fairly cup in the hands. In the xinwei year, when the candidates assembled for the capital, there were ten of us, fellow countrymen of Jiashan. Only Ding Jingyu, whose courtesy name was Bin, was the youngest, and he was exceedingly humble. I said to Fei Jinpo: “This brother is certain to pass this year.” Fei said: “How can you tell?” I said: “It is the humble alone who receive blessing. Do you see, among the ten, any who is as earnest and gracious, never putting himself before others, as Jingyu? Any who is as reverent and compliant, as careful and humble and awed, as Jingyu? Any who, when insulted, does not answer, and, when slandered, does not argue back, as Jingyu? A man who can be like this — Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits, will surely protect him. How could he fail to rise?” When the list was posted, Ding indeed passed. In the dingchou year I was in the capital and lodged together with Feng Kaizhi. I saw him empty himself and compose his countenance, greatly changed from the habits of his youth. Li Jiyan, a straightforward and trustworthy friend, at times attacked his faults to his face, and I saw only that he received it with a level heart and compliant acceptance, never answering with a single word. I said to him: “Blessing has its beginning, and calamity has its forerunner. If this heart is truly humble, Heaven will surely assist it. You are certain to pass this year.” And so it proved. Zhao Yufeng, whose courtesy name was Guangyuan, was a man of Guanxian in Shandong. In his youth he passed the provincial examination, but for a long time he did not pass the higher one. His father was the third assistant magistrate of Jiashan, and he accompanied him to his post. Admiring Qian Mingwu, he brought his essays to show him. Mingwu crossed out every one of them, and Zhao not only was not angry but was convinced at heart and quickly amended them. The following year he passed the examination. In the renchen year I went to court and met Xia Jiansuo. I saw that his manner was modest and his bearing lowly, and the glow of humility pressed upon others. Returning, I told a friend: “Whenever Heaven is about to raise up such a man, before it issues his blessing it first issues his wisdom. Once this wisdom is issued, the flighty of themselves become solid, and the unrestrained of themselves draw back. Jiansuo is gentle and good like this; Heaven has opened him.” When the list was posted, he indeed passed.

Zhang Weiyan of Jiangyin had accumulated much learning and was skilled in letters, and he had a name among the literary circles. At the provincial examination held in Nanjing in the jiawu year he lodged in a temple. When the results were announced his name was not among them, and he roundly cursed the examiners, declaring that they were blind. It happened that a Daoist priest stood nearby, smiling. Zhang at once turned his anger upon the priest. The priest said: “Your essay, sir, must surely have been poor.” Zhang, more enraged, said: “You have not seen my essay — how do you know it was poor?” The priest said: “I have heard that in writing an essay what matters most is a heart and spirit at peace. Now I hear you railing and cursing — you are far from at peace. How could your essay be well made?” Zhang could not but yield, and so drew near and asked his instruction. The priest said: “Passing depends wholly on destiny. If destiny does not decree that you should pass, then though your essay be well made it is of no avail. You must make a turning about in yourself.” Zhang said: “If it is destiny, how can there be a turning about?” The priest said: “He who makes destiny is Heaven; he who establishes destiny is myself. Strive in good deeds and broadly accumulate hidden virtue — what blessing could not be sought?” Zhang said: “I am a poor scholar. What can I do?” The priest said: “Good deeds and hidden merit are all made by the mind. If you constantly keep this mind, your merit and virtue will be beyond measure. Take humility alone, for instance: it costs not a copper. Why do you not look into yourself instead of cursing the examiners?” From this Zhang bowed his will, restrained himself, each day added to his cultivation of good, and each day thickened his virtue. In the dingyou year he dreamed that he came to a tall building and obtained a register of examination results, in which many rows were missing. He asked a bystander: “This is the register of this year’s examination — why are so many names missing?” The answer came: “The underworld reviews examination ranks once every three years, and only those who have accumulated virtue and are without fault may have their names entered. Those missing, as before, are all men who by former reckoning should have passed, but who, because of some recent meanness of conduct, have been struck off.” Then the man pointed to one row and said: “For three years past you have been rather careful in your conduct; perhaps you may fill this place. Take good care of yourself.” That year he indeed passed, at number one hundred and five. From this we see that three feet above a man’s head there are surely spirits and gods, and that to hasten toward good fortune and shun misfortune rests decisively with oneself. We must so order our hearts and govern our conduct as not to offend Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits, in the smallest degree, and with an emptied heart and a humbled self so to conduct ourselves that Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits, may at every moment take pity on us; only thus is there a foundation for receiving blessing. A man puffed full of pride is certainly no vessel for far things; even should he rise, he will have no enjoyment of it. A scholar of but slight insight and experience will surely not have the heart to narrow his own measure and shut out his own blessing. How much more so, since humility gives ground for receiving instruction and draws good without end — how could it be anything but indispensable to one who cultivates his work? An old saying has it: “He who has set his will on rank and emolument will surely obtain rank and emolument; he who has set his will on wealth and honor will surely obtain wealth and honor.” A man’s will is like a tree’s root. Let him fix this will firmly, and then with thought upon thought be humble, and in dust after dust be skillful in means; he will of himself move Heaven and Earth, and blessing will be made by him. Those today who seek to pass the examinations have never truly had a will at the outset; it is no more than a passing mood. When the mood comes they seek, and when the mood flags they stop. Mencius said: “If the king loved music greatly, how near might Qi not be to good order?” The same holds, I think, for examination rank.

A man’s evil is by nature not something he was born with. Once the habits of long defilement have sunk deep, he rushes on and none can save him; sometimes he knows clearly and offends on purpose, sometimes he offends in ignorance by mistake. Tracing it to its outcome, he has built up a crime that fills the heavens; tracing it to its beginning, it came only from a single thought that went astray. Yet in the still of night the Heaven-given conscience is present in every man. At the moment when his road first goes wrong and his evil thought first stirs, if one warns him in earnest words and strives with all one’s might to hold him back, who is so devoid of heart that he will not change his course and follow good? Or again, in the unhappy case of one whose evil is already notorious, if I can with utter sincerity move and transform him, check him, and stop him, is it not possible that a good heart may well up in him of itself and wash away a thousand transgressions at a stroke? No man is a sage or a worthy, so how can every word and deed of his be good? If there is a single word or deed worth taking, one should praise and commend it, so that those already good may be confirmed in their resolve and brought to completion, and those not yet good may hear of it, admire, and be stirred to rise. Is this not to accord with the decree of Heaven? Yu Tiejiao said: To check means to use force to stop it, and not merely to gloss over it in silence. To praise means to extol it with all one’s voice, and of guiding, supporting, rewarding, and encouraging there is no need even to speak. This is the compassion for the wicked and the delight in the good showing itself in action.

The Daoists say: check evil and praise good. The Buddhists say: stop evil and practice good. The Confucians say: conceal evil and praise good. The words of the three teachings come forth as from one mouth. From this we know that the mind-substance of the sages is empty, numinous, and utterly clear, not a shred of desire remaining in it, like a bright mirror reflecting forms, which reflects as it comes and transforms as it reflects. Therefore when they see evil it of itself melts away, and when they see good it is of itself made bright. To check and to praise are nothing other than the restoring of sentient beings to their original nature-substance.

Yu Shun was on the riverbank when he saw fishermen contending for the deep pools and rich marshes, while the old and weak fished the shallow shoals and racing currents. He was moved to pity for them, and went to fish there himself. When he saw the contentious, he hid their faults and did not speak of them; when he saw those who yielded, he praised them and took them as his model. Within a year all were yielding the deep pools and rich marshes to one another. The great Shun joined with others in doing good, and it was simply a single intent of joyful encouragement; therefore the measure of his good was without end. This is what a sage is, and beyond our reach. Yet here is one saying by which a student of the lower learning who takes it up may reach the higher. Check your own evil, and only then can you check the evil of others. Praise the good of others, and only then can you encourage the good in others.

What this passage points to is very broad: for instance, brothers dividing an inheritance, or friends dealing in money and property, and the like. Yet between brothers the bond is one of heavenly kinship, while wealth is an outward thing; how much more should one yield it up. The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching says: “The man of many desires, because he seeks much profit, has much affliction as well. The man of few desires, seeking nothing and desiring nothing, has no such trouble. If you would escape all afflictions, you should contemplate contentment. The way of contentment is itself the place of wealth, joy, peace, and security. The contented man, though he lie upon the ground, is still at peace and happy; the discontented man, though he dwell in heaven, is still not satisfied.” Thus we know that if a man can press the many upon others and take the few for himself, his mind will of itself be level and calm, and meeting circumstances nothing will invade him, and he will always walk in contentment.

Yu Tiejiao said: Wealth is the primal vital force of Heaven and Earth. The government of Yao and Shun was the enriching of the people; the way to bring peace to the world is the ordering of wealth. A man living in this world cannot live without wealth, and there is no man who does not love wealth, nor any day on which wealth is not used. It is thus something indispensable, and thus a sum that can never be abundant. Yet the temperament each man has in the use of wealth leans to its own extreme. The spendthrift tosses away a thousand pieces of gold at a single throw; the miser will not pluck out a single hair. The man of integrity refuses it in the darkness of night; the greedy and overbearing seize it in broad daylight. Now the spendthrift and the man of integrity are both of them fair names, yet neither may exceed due measure. Let the spendthrift exceed it, and the bed’s head is emptied and there is nothing to continue with; let the man of integrity exceed it, and morning and evening go wanting and those above and below are resentful. Between the miser and the greedy and overbearing there is a greater distance, but the miser’s insight is shallow and mean: he treasures every scruple and dram, like a bee guarding its honey or a small child clutching his cake, unwilling to share out the least part with another. Yet he is still but keeping what is his own; therefore men dislike him, but Heaven does not deeply resent him. The greedy and overbearing, however, would obtain what was never theirs at all, and here there is no limit. Like a fish swallowing a boat, like a snake swallowing an elephant; brothers contend, friends become enemies, brigands kill men, corrupt officials bend the law, treacherous ministers sell the state — all are done by the single thought of greed. This book warns against the calamity of greed for wealth more than once and more than twice. Yet to warn men against taking wrongly, and then to teach them flatly not to take at all, would never do. Therefore it sets before them the two words “much” and “little,” that a man may weigh his own portion and make this the right way of obtaining wealth. The measure of much and little has no fixed standard: to the poor a single piece of gold is not little, to the rich ten thousand pieces of gold are not much; the man of integrity, entitled to a hundred, may take ten and not feel it little, while the greedy man, entitled to a hundred, may take a thousand and not call it much. Only with a level heart and a just mind, measuring the sum that I ought to receive and taking no more than my portion, is the way of taking little. Yet the human heart is troubled by having little and longs for much — this is the common temper. If a man can but follow circumstances without contending, he is already not bad. But to make him see much and instead press it away — is this not contrary to human feeling? Ah, there is a reason for it. Wealth comes by more than one road. The wealth that lies ready to hand may not be what is allotted to me in my destiny; and the hidden decree is after all impossible to examine and verify. Should it by any chance not be what my destiny holds, then it is tainted meat and poisoned wine — can it fill the belly? Therefore it is best to press it away. If it is not what destiny holds and one presses it away, one may indeed escape fault; and even if it is what destiny holds and one mistakenly presses it away, it will surely come again by another road. Take care not to prove unable to endure, and so act rashly over what lies before your eyes. This is easier for the rich and noble, and harder for the poor and lowly. To know its difficulty and still strive in it, so that ghosts and spirits may witness this one thought of not daring to act rashly, then though one’s place be hard and difficult, one should not come to the misery of having no means to live. Believe it truly and hold it firmly, and the way of taking little is itself the way of growing rich.

Xu Ji of the Song dynasty, dividing the family property with his two uncles, first asked his two uncles to take all that they desired, leaving only a single chest of books and two dilapidated rooms, and Ji received them with a glad heart.

In Cixi, two friends were on good terms. A obtained a teaching post with a fee of nine taels, and B also obtained a post, with a fee of only six taels. A said joyfully: “Next year neither of us need worry about those at home.” B said: “You have only your honored sister-in-law at home, brother, and nine taels is more than enough for your needs; I, however, have my father and mother above me, and six taels is not yet sufficient.” A said: “So be it.” And he yielded his own post to B and himself took B’s post. After arriving at the school he picked up from under the bed a damaged book in which were copied several prescriptions for external medicine, and his pupil said it was a relic left by the former teacher. In winter he returned home and saw several servants in a great flurry, urgently asking whether there was a practitioner of external medicine in that place. On inquiry he learned: “Our master, traveling from Fujian to take up the post of provincial administration commissioner in Shandong, was suddenly afflicted with a sore on his back and suffers agony past bearing; it has been three days now.” A remembered the prescriptions and saw that they exactly matched this condition, and so went along with them. Applying moxa according to the prescriptions, the man was indeed cured. The commissioner was overjoyed and rewarded him with a hundred taels. When the talk turned to how he had yielded the teaching post and so obtained the prescriptions, the commissioner praised him with great admiration. It happened that the magistrate of Cixi was his year-nephew, and he recommended him with all his strength, so that he was admitted into the prefectural school. Ah, brothers of the same blood will still contend over wealth — how much more so friends? To think that a friend could not support his father, and so to press the many upon him and take the few for oneself: three taels is a small thing, but such righteousness is loftier than a thousand chariots. In the end he reaped both name and profit, all of it coming from a single thought of yielding. Those who eagerly contend for gain and turn hostile at the slightest thing — can they look on this without shame?

When disgrace comes, one should only ask oneself: does the fault lie with me? Then disgrace is what I deserve. Does the fault lie with the other? Then this disgrace is undeserved — and if it does not truly disgrace me, it is no disgrace at all. It is not that one ought not to resent it; it is that there is in truth nothing to resent. From of old, the greatly wise and the greatly brave have always been able to endure small shames and small angers, and only so could they bear great matters and accomplish great deeds. How could this be known to one of narrow and shallow measure?

Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty, a man of Pinghu, admonished the younger members of his family, saying: No man who has not set himself to the practice of forbearance can ever know how hard the word forbearance is; and no man who has not weighed the two thoughts of good and evil against each other can ever know how wondrous the word forbearance is. If a man cannot bear shame and endure hardship, then even though he have a good heart, one provocation will burst it and one setback will bring it down. When Heaven is about to lay a great charge upon such a man, it must first stir his heart and steel his nature, until it would have every man pass through this gate. Broadly speaking, in giving relief to others one need not mind receiving their anger; in planning for others one need not refuse their resentment and reproach. Undertaking affairs requires that one bear with resentment; in transforming others by persuasion one need not stoop to mockery and censure. To have a heart of generosity and forbearance may bring one ridicule and insult — these come in the same bundle with it. One who does not discern this root is no man of good.

Li Hang of the Song dynasty, as prime minister, had a wild fellow who seized his horse’s bridle and presented him with a letter, in which he roundly vilified his faults. Li declined and thanked him, saying: “When I return I shall read it carefully.” The wild fellow, enraged, reviled him, saying: “You sit in high office, yet you cannot bring peace and relief to the world, and you do not withdraw into retirement. You have long blocked the road of worthy men — are you not ashamed in your heart?” The duke, on horseback, bowed and said with unease: “I have repeatedly sought to retire, but alas, my sovereign has not granted it, and I dare not act on my own convenience.” To the end he showed no sign of anger.

In the Song dynasty Wen Yanbo served as first minister. The censor Tang Jie impeached him, saying that while Yanbo was prefect of Yizhou he had woven rare brocade and made his way into the palace apartments, and by such means obtained the office of chief councillor, and he asked that he be dismissed. The emperor was angry and meant to send Tang Jie into distant exile. At that time Yanbo stood before the emperor, and Tang Jie reproached him to his face, saying: “Yanbo, you should examine yourself; if the thing was indeed done, you must not conceal it.” Yanbo bowed in apology without ceasing, and the emperor grew angrier still, degrading Tang Jie to assistant prefect of Yingzhou and dismissing Yanbo as prefect of Xuzhou. Later Yanbo again became chief councillor, and he said to the emperor: “Tang Jie was a censor, and in speaking of my affairs he mostly struck at my real faults; among them there may have been errors born of hearsay, yet at the time I reproached him too deeply.” Thereupon Tang Jie was summoned to be director of the Remonstrance Bureau. People of the time called Yanbo a man of generous spirit. He served through the three reigns of Yingzong, Shenzong, and Zhezong, holding the office of Grand Preceptor and managing the weighty affairs of state, his rank above that of the chief councillors, and he was enfeoffed as Duke of Lu. For fifty years he served as general and minister; his name was heard among the four barbarian nations, and he died at the age of ninety-two.

Fu Bi of the Song instructed his sons and younger brothers, saying: “The one word forbearance is the gate of all wonders. If to purity and frugality one adds forbearance, what affair cannot be accomplished?” When he was young, a man reviled him.
