Someone said: “He is reviling you.” Bi said: “Perhaps he is reviling another.” The man said: “He called your name and surname and reviled you.” Bi said: “Are there not in the world others of the same name and surname?” When the reviler heard this he was greatly ashamed. Yan Guangzhou said: The one word forbearance is the hardest of all. While one is able to forbear, one’s virtue and measure must be great; by the time one cannot forbear, the breath of pride and privilege has already overflowed. An ancient poem says: “The youth beneath men’s legs took no offense; the old man at the bridge was startled and ill at ease. If in a life one looked not to the waning years, why should Huaiyin be counted less than Wencheng?” How true these words are! Han Xin was made a king through bearing the shame beneath men’s legs, and perished through scorning the Marquis of Jiang and Fan Kuai. When one has drunk to the full measure, nothing more can of course be added.

Peng Ju of Taizhou was kind, gentle, and humble. He once lodged in an inn together with a certain man; Peng returned home early, and the man lost his umbrella and supposed that Peng had carried it off. He came to Peng’s gate and cursed him in anger; seeing that Peng was timid, he further declared that he had lost clothing and demanded its price. Peng repaid him the full sum, and he went away. A neighbor who relied on his strength encroached upon Peng’s land, and Peng left it unquestioned. Later the neighbor became entangled in a lawsuit through his own violence, and Peng instead worked on his behalf so that he escaped. His other good deeds were very many. Because he had no son, he went to the Western shrine to pray for an heir, and in a dream a spirit said to him: “Because you bear insult with patience and are kind and gentle, and earnestly practice good deeds, your petition has been granted.” Thereupon he had three sons. Later, when the troubles of Shu came, nine households out of ten perished, yet Peng alone, with his whole family, came through unharmed.

Old Mr. Xia of Jiangyin was playing chess with a guest when suddenly a man came rushing in roaring: “I owe your household only two taels of interest silver — why do you have your people press me day after day?” Before the old man could answer, the man cursed him loudly and overturned the table, ruining the chessboard. The old man laughed and said: “Do you wish for a release?” He at once took up his brush and gave him a written waiver. The man hurried off with thanks, and the guest sighed at his great virtue. The old man said: “Forbearance is the gate of all wonders. Whenever one moves through the world and deals with things, if violence and perversity are laid upon me, it is like walking among thorns: walk slowly and loosen them, and what is there in the thorns to be angry at? Or again, it is like an empty boat colliding with me, or a falling tile striking me; then the mind is untroubled and resentment can be dissolved. Besides, this man’s looks were fierce and his words foolish; he must have had something to rely upon, and I feared that to provoke him would bring about some unforeseen turn. So I leniently released him.” That evening word came that the man had died in a privy. On careful inquiry into the matter it was learned that this man, driven by debt and with no way out, had taken poison and come intending to contrive a swindle; but moved by Old Mr. Xia’s lenient release, he could not bear to work the fraud, and so hurried home to seek the excrement antidote for the poison. Yet the drug’s force broke out violently and there was no time left to counteract it. The old man bowed to Heaven in thanks, and all men respected and submitted to him. Had the old man not ordinarily extinguished his fiery temper and deeply cultivated self-restraint, how could he have held himself so steady at such a moment? Now, bearing insult is indeed essential to cultivating the person; and next to it, the key to preserving wealth likewise lies in learning to take a loss.

Wang Hong, Duke Zhuangyi of the Ming, courtesy name Gongdu, when he established his headquarters at Yangzhou, had a subordinate official, a certain Shan, whose conduct was unregulated; the duke had once rebuked and repressed him. It happened that the duke was censured and returned home, and passing by the place where Shan held office, Shan waited to see him off, sending generous gifts of food. The duke, thinking well of his sincere good will, selected and accepted several jars, taking them for sauce and vinegar. When he opened them, they were all filth. Before long his affair was cleared and he returned to office; Shan fled, and had his family falsely announce that he was dead. An enemy tracked him down, seized him, and brought a suit against him before the duke. The duke only settled the suit amicably and released him.

I respectfully observe that in the Nirvana Sutra there was once a man who praised the Buddha as having the marks of great merit. Someone said: “How do you see it?” He said: “His years and his resolve were both at their height, yet he was not violent; struck, he was not angered; reviled, he was not wrathful. Are these not the marks of great merit?” When people today are faced with violence and perversity, let them only say: “He has come to perfect my marks of merit” — what honor could be greater? Then on my side I can be wronged without contending, and on his side he too will be transformed and awakened.

Zheng Xuan said: Be still, be still, be still — hence countless immortals win their will. Forgive, forgive, forgive — a thousand woes, ten thousand ills at once relieve. Endure, endure, endure — hence creditor and foeman hide them evermore. Cease, cease, cease — the fame that fills the world is never free.

When honor and favor come to one, though they be what one’s lot deserves, one should still know the moment and know contentment, with a sense of being unable to bear the weight, as if startled and afraid. For blessing is that on which calamity leans; when the sun is at noon it declines, when the moon is full it wanes — such is the nature of things. As for the ruler above, his grace is like heaven and earth; if one does not truly seek to repay it, how can a subject rest easy? Would that not leave him the more alarmed?

King Cheng of Zhou enfeoffed Boqin in Lu, and the Duke of Zhou admonished him, saying: “Do not by reason of the state of Lu treat others with arrogance. I have heard it said: he whose virtue is broad and great, yet who keeps himself with courtesy, is honored; he whose lands are wide and rich, yet who keeps himself with frugality, is secure; he whose rank and emoluments are lofty and glorious, yet who keeps himself lowly, is exalted; he whose people are many and soldiers strong, yet who keeps himself in fear, is victorious; he who is wise and understanding, yet who keeps himself as though dull, profits; he who has heard much and remembers much, yet who keeps himself as though shallow, is enlarged. These are the six keepings, and all are the virtue of humility. The way of Heaven destroys the full and increases the humble; the way of Earth alters the full and flows toward the humble; the way of men hates the full and loves the humble. Be careful, then, and do not by reason of the state of Lu treat others with arrogance.” If students today can truly ponder and unfold this instruction, then a proud heart and an arrogant temper will have no place to arise in them, and when honor and favor are bestowed they will at all times have the sense of being startled.

Cen Wenben of the Tang was appointed Director of the Secretariat and wore a troubled look. His mother asked him, and Wenben said: “I am neither a man of merit nor an old retainer, yet I presumptuously enjoy honor and favor; my position is high and my responsibility heavy, and therefore I am anxious and afraid.” He said to the guests who came to congratulate him: “Today I receive condolences, not congratulations.” Wang Dan, Duke Wenzheng of the Song, in his later years held ever more honored office, and when he was made envoy to Korea he rode in a carriage from within the palace and out the capital gate, while the hundred officials feasted him farewell and with one voice called his lot glorious. The duke said: “What have I done for the state? I only feel restless and ill at ease.” Sima Wengong wrote in a letter to his nephew: “I have lately received the imperial grace and been appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery, while through the whole court there are countless who envy me; and with my blunt honesty placed among them, I am like a yellow leaf in a fierce wind — how long before it falls? Therefore, since receiving the charge, I have had fear and no joy. You should understand this intent.” These several lords were all of the sort who, receiving favor, are as if startled; and as for Lord Cen’s one phrase about receiving condolences, its meaning should be unfolded. Formerly, when Sunshu Ao was chief minister, an old man came to offer condolences, saying: “He who by reason of his nobility treats others with arrogance — the people leave him. He who by reason of his high position monopolizes power — the ruler hates him. He who by reason of his rich emoluments knows no contentment — calamity settles upon him.” And he added: “Let your position be ever higher and your mind ever lower; let your office be ever greater and your mind ever smaller; and when your emoluments are already rich, be cautious and dare not take more. If you carefully keep these three, you are sufficient to govern Chu.” Lord Cen had indeed grasped this meaning deeply, and the method of dwelling on high truly lies in this.

Lu Duoxun of the Song, when first appointed Assistant Administrator, became gradually lavish in his dress and furnishings. His father said with a sorrowful look: “Our family for generations has been poor scholars; in a single day we have come to wealth and honor, and already it is like this. I do not know where the carriage will at last be unhitched.” Duoxun gave no thought to his father’s words, and in the end was ruined by an affair.

To bestow kindness and seek repayment is to have not forgotten a greedy heart; to regret what one has given is to have not transformed a stingy heart. Greedy and stingy at once — the noble man does not do so. The Diamond Sutra says: “A bodhisattva, in regard to dharmas, should give without dwelling in anything.” It also says: “If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in signs, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.” From this we see that when a man can aid others with his wealth, inwardly not seeing a self that gives, outwardly not seeing a person who receives, and in between not seeing the thing given, this is called the threefold wheel being empty and the one mind pure. Then a measure of grain is reckoned a boundless blessing, and a single coin dissolves the calamities of a thousand kalpas. But if there be the least thought of seeking repayment, though one give ten thousand pieces of gold, it will in the end not fill the measure of the one mind. As for the two words regret — this above all is a great hinge in human life. If one regrets an evil deed, then future evil thoughts gradually cease; if one regrets a good deed, then future good thoughts will not arise. If a man gives and then regrets it, it were better for him not to have given at all.

When people of the world wish to have grain in their granaries without lack year after year, they must take seed of grain and wheat, and with ox and plough till the fields and plant them; if they do not plant, it is exhausted. So too is it in the Dharma. Take the heart of filial piety, the heart of compassion, and the heart of reverence as the seed; take clothing and food, wealth and silk, body and life as the ox and plough; take parents, the poor and sick, and the Three Treasures as the field. If a disciple of the Buddha wishes to have within the storehouse consciousness the hundred blessings adorned and inexhaustible life after life, he must set in motion the hearts of compassion, reverence, and filial piety, and with clothing, food, wealth, silk, body, and life reverently support and supply parents, the poor and sick, and the Three Treasures — this is called planting blessing. If one does not plant, then one is poor and destitute, without blessing or wisdom, and enters the perilous road of birth and death. The field of planting blessing is like the field of planting grain, and it is called the field of blessing.

Giving is of three kinds: there is the giving of Dharma, the giving of wealth, and the giving of the mind. By various skillful means to exhort, transform, teach, and instruct people is called the giving of Dharma, and it is the highest good. The giving of wealth means giving all kinds of money and goods. As for the giving of the mind, it is when one is straitened by having no wealth, and merely in the heart feels compassion and wishes to relieve another yet has no means to do so — this too is called giving.

Shen Li of the Ming, courtesy name Zhonghua, a native of Guide, loved to advance worthy scholars without letting others know. He had words to warn the world, saying: “Alas! How uneven are the affairs of the world! When I am at a guest banquet, drunk and full, unable to lift another chopstick, and the host still presses rare delicacies upon me without end — yet there are poor folk who to the end of their lives never know a rare flavor, and some who die of hunger. I wear fur in winter and hemp in summer, cool or warm according to the season, yet still would exhaust luxury and extravagance to follow the fashion — while there are poor folk whose clothes do not cover their bodies, who sleep in the dew beside the eaves, the north wind piercing their bones, shivering and their teeth chattering. I dwell at ease in high eaves and great beams, yet still make ponds and terraces, flowers and bamboos, exhausting the pleasures of eye and ear, grudging not a thousand pieces of gold to buy them — while poor folk, in urgent need and with nothing to rely upon, come even to cast away their lives and cut off the joys of father and son, husband and wife. My own person, my household, and my descendants are already amply provided, yet still I labor to accumulate much and store deeply, making long plans for my descendants — while there are poor folk whose rooms are like a hanging chime-stone, who cannot plan at evening for the morning. My goods and wealth are in confusion and abundance, and my eyes and ears cannot attend to all of it, so that it unavoidably comes to waste, secretly enriching thieves — yet when a poor man happens to pick up a leftover sheaf or a stray ear of grain, I can bear not to give it. Or when someone owes me interest on a loan, or in exchanging labor and goods, over the tip of a knife-blade or an awl-point there are those who strive with all their might. I spread out baskets and platters and cling to the powerful and noble, fearing only that they will not accept — yet when a poor man begs a single coin to prolong his life a day and a night, there are those who flush with anger. There are those who entrust themselves to one’s inmost heart, yet one cannot take them in because they are poor. I have much wealth, display extravagance, and lead others into excess, and thereby purchase calamity — while there are poor folk who wait for the scraps of my rat-holes and cannot get them. How is it that the affairs of the world are so uneven, to such a degree as this! I now plead for the poor — not that I would, by such means as pouring out one’s whole fortune to relieve famine, force men to do what is hard, but only that they give up what is useless to them and turn it into what is useful. If at a guest banquet one is drunk and full, why not divide the cups and goblets and give to those who are starving and near death? Why not divide the leftover broth and give to those who in all their lives have never known a rare flavor? Would that not be convenient for both? Clothes that lie worn out in chests and boxes are the same as no clothes; spare out a coarse short jacket to give to those whose clothes do not cover their bodies, and they will be as warm as if wrapped in silk floss, while my own embroidered robes will not on that account be lacking. If I do not make playthings for eye and ear, I can preserve a man’s life and his own flesh and blood — this is a righteous deed. It furnishes matter for talk and may be handed down; it gives one peace in the still watches of the night and brings its own contentment. Of all things in the world that may be enjoyed, none is better than this. To accumulate much and store deeply, not to use it all in one’s whole life, and to leave it to one’s sons and grandsons: then the worthy will not depend on it and will yet have enough, while the foolish, though they get it, will make no use of it. Why not, in my own lifetime, give it to those who cannot plan at evening for the morning? That would still be of use. As for what I have let go to waste, it is already put out of my reckoning; if a poor man gets it, it is picking up what was dropped on the road, not diminishing what I have. Why should I begrudge it? I spread out lavish things and cling to the mighty — will that ever be counted as virtue? To give a pint or a peck to one in a dried-up wheel-rut brings joy and raises the dead to life. Why not do this instead of that? When I have much wealth it works mischief for me; when he gets a little it becomes blessing for him. And when I diminish my surplus to supply his lack, though I bring blessing to another, I in truth escape calamity myself — this is the way that profits both. Therefore I say: to give up the useless to become the useful — this is it. Do you not observe the way of Heaven and the affairs of men? Waxing and waning, diminishing and growing — even Heaven does not oppose it. Money and goods flow in circulation; how should they stay in one place? Of the rich houses once renowned, how many survive today? Their sons and grandsons did not enjoy it to the end. It is not because their forebears loved to give and made no far-reaching plans; prosperity and decline lean upon each other — the force of circumstance makes it so. He who knows this, and so accumulates when it is right to accumulate and disperses when it is right to disperse, so that it may be used for himself and may also be used for others — such a one is a man of understanding. He who cages money and goods, gathers them into one room, and sets up dikes against them, taking them for a business unshakable for ten million generations, so that they can find no other channel of flow — such a one is a fool. He who accumulates hidden virtue with a view to what is lasting is a wise man. He who acts without acting for anything is a noble man.”

Li Shiqian of the Sui, courtesy name Ziyue, was orphaned young and served his mother with utmost filial piety. At the age of twelve the Prince of Guangping of Wei summoned him to be a military aide in his establishment. His family was rich, and he brought out several thousand piculs of grain to lend to his fellow villagers. When the year turned poor, he summoned each debtor and burned the bonds, saying: “The debt is settled.” The next spring he again brought out seed grain and distributed it to the poor and needy. Those he saved were very many, and he buried the dead. Someone praised his hidden virtue, and he said: “Hidden virtue is like a ringing in the ear: one alone knows it, and no man knows of it. Now that you already know it, how can it be called hidden virtue?” One day he dreamed that a spirit in purple robes told him: “Heaven commends your hidden virtue; it will make your descendants flourish and great.”

A man of the Gu family of Taicang in the Song was a clerk of the prefecture, and whenever he had to escort or welcome officials he always lodged with the Jiang family, cake-sellers outside the city wall. Later Jiang was incited by an enemy to harbor bandits; Gu gathered the people and appealed his grievance so that he was released. Jiang was grateful, and having a daughter of seventeen, sent her to Gu’s house, wishing her to be his concubine. Gu had his wife prepare gifts and send her back; Jiang brought her again, and Gu once more declined and returned her. Later Gu went to the capital and was assigned to serve under Vice Minister Han. It happened that the vice minister went out, and his lady saw Gu and summoned him, asking: “Are you not Gu the controller of Taicang? I am the daughter of the Jiang family who sold cakes. I was married as the lord’s junior consort, and before long became his principal wife — every hair of it was your gift. I should speak of it to the lord.” When the vice minister returned, she told him the whole story from beginning to end. The vice minister said: “He is a man of humanity.” In the end he reported the matter, and the emperor praised and sighed over it, and appointed Gu a principal secretary of the Ministry of Rites.

Fan Wenzheng of the Song sent his son Yaofu back to Suzhou to fetch five hundred piculs of wheat. On the way he met his father’s old friend Shi Manqing, who spoke of three funerals that could not be carried out. Yaofu gave him the whole boat of wheat. When he returned home he had not yet had time to speak of it when Wenzheng said: “Did you see my old friend?” Yaofu answered that Shi Manqing had three funerals that could not be carried out. Wenzheng said: “Why did you not give him the boat of wheat?” He replied: “I did give it.” Thus the Fan father and son were of one mind, delighting in giving to this degree. How unlike the people of today, who only pay honor to the rich and noble, adding flowers to brocade, and will not relieve the poor and suffering with timely aid, sending charcoal in the snow! And even if there be one who gives a little and bestows a little, is there any who does not seek repayment or regret it?

Formerly a woman came to a temple wishing to give, but she had no wealth, only two coins. She donated them, and the one in charge of the temple himself performed the confession for her. Later, when she had entered the palace and become rich and honored, she brought several thousand pieces of gold to the temple and gave it, yet the presiding monk only had his disciple transfer the merit. Astonished, she asked him about it, and the monk said: “Before, the gift was slight but the heart was utterly true, so this old monk performed the confession himself. Now the gift is heavy but the heart is not earnest; it is enough to have my disciple do the confession in my place.” Now in doing good and planting virtue, the utmost sincerity of heart is what matters most; once the thought turns, it is already not as the first thought was — how much less if one regrets it!

Yu Tieqiao said: Even birds and beasts know to repay kindness — how could there be a man who does not feel gratitude? But he does not know that what is hardest to bear is the look of a benefactor. Once that look is revealed, the one who feels gratitude is shamed, and shame turns and resentment is born. Formerly there was a clerk who had once saved a man’s life. The man gradually grew rich while the clerk in turn grew poor. Chancing to pass by his house, the whole family came out to bow to him, and pressed him to drink with the greatest respect. When the clerk was flushed with wine he said loudly: “Had it not been for my effort, would your wife and children, your maids and servants, and all the things now before your eyes, be one of them yours? Now you are rich and I on the contrary am poor — why is that?” Having spoken, he lodged at the man’s house. The man reckoned thus: “His hope of repayment is too extravagant; to repay him cannot satisfy him. If I do not repay him, calamity will surely come upon me. Better to kill him.” So he strangled him. Alas! To save a man and thereby bring about one’s own death — herein there was of itself a cause of converging and cunning coincidence. The man’s fierce, evil retribution and the clerk’s fated span of life must be so; let these be set aside and not discussed. I raise this case only to warn those who seek repayment.

From here to “the immortals may be hoped for,” the text speaks of the blessings that come to the good man, great and unfailing. Now the reality of the good man begins with not erring in right and wrong, whereby wisdom and courage are both fulfilled, and ends with forgetting both self and others, whereby benevolence and forbearance are both practiced. How much more does he, in establishing his mind and applying his intent, in his dealings with himself and with others, inwardly in the five constants and the hundred practices, outwardly in affairs and things and their proper occasions, leave nothing unfulfilled? Even were Yao and Shun, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius to be born again, they would be no different from this. Yet he is merely called a good man, because the heart of Heaven loves good and hates evil, and the heart of man has good and no evil. Men are ever careless of the taint of habit and so lose their original state. When there is good, one should advance in it with vigor; when there is evil, one should reform and repent — then one is near to it.

Li Fang, Duke Wenzheng of the Song, after retiring from office, was sent for by Emperor Taizong on the occasion of the Lantern Festival, who ordered a cushioned carriage to bring him, seated him beside the imperial couch, poured wine for him with his own hand from the imperial flagon, and chose the choicest of the fruits and nuts to bestow on him, saying: “You are a good man and a noble man. Twice you have held the office of chief councillor, and never once had a heart to wound others or harm creatures — this is why I think of you.” When the duke returned home he instructed his sons, saying: “Though I have no extraordinary merit or great achievement to astonish the world and startle the vulgar, yet I have never covered over another’s good nor forgotten another’s advancement; I have not deceived in a dark chamber; I have measured my virtue and kept to my lot. In these four things I may claim to have walked aright. Now I am honored that His Majesty, before the assembled ministers, should praise me as a good man and a noble man. But of the good man and the noble man, even Confucius said that he had not seen one — what manner of man am I, that I should dare to bear the name? You should keep in mind His Majesty’s words of high commendation, and practice my four sayings: be loyal to your lord, filial to your parents, cultivated and careful, standing on your own — thus perhaps you may be without shame.” His son Zong’e reverently kept his forebear’s instruction and became a man of note in his time. Now the good man, to speak of him lightly, is one who stops evil and does good; to speak of him at the utmost, he realizes sagehood and becomes a Perfected, exhausts the spirit and penetrates transformation — all of it is but this one good thought carried to fullness.

Zou Ziyin of Jiangxi in the Ming dynasty revered and believed in the Three Treasures and diligently practiced the hundred good deeds. Whenever he rescued anyone from trouble or helped anyone accomplish a good work, though it meant scalding water and fire, cold or heat, he did not decline. People called him a good man. When he died of illness and came before Lord Yama, his heart was unconvinced, and Yama ordered a clerk to open the register and show it to him. When the register was opened, there were at once two great words: fame and profit. Every good deed Ziyin had done in his life was either recorded under the word fame or entered under the word profit. Ziyin was ashamed and submitted. Reviving, he said to people: “Tell all who do good, on my behalf, that they should be truly sincere and earnest, and sweep their minds clean.” Five days later he died. Tang Shi said: I knew Ziyin in detail; a love of fame he perhaps could not avoid. But as for profit — Ziyin was a man who made light of wealth and upheld righteousness; how could he have this? It must be that when he acted as middleman or was asked to intercede, his first thought was to vow good, but by the time the money and goods came into his hands he occasionally borrowed from them; or he said at first, “I will borrow it for a time,” and afterward kept it long on loan and never returned it. And so Ziyin, for all the toil of a lifetime, won only these two words. From this one may see that the underworld tribunals are wont to record the hidden, subtle, and indirect accounts. I understand Ziyin’s intent and make it known for him; and therefore I tell all who do good: to act without acting for anything, and yet to leave nothing undone, benefiting beings according to circumstance — this is the highest. To have no thought of seeking reward, to rescue suffering beings and urge others to do good — this is next. To broadly accumulate hidden merit and seek to escape the three evil paths for oneself — this is next again. If there be the least thought of fame, one has already taken the wrong road; and if there be the least thought of privately fattening one’s own purse, then one enters hell swift as an arrow. Should one not tremble? I record this in hope that those who hereafter wish to be good men may discern clearly and practice earnestly.

Goodness is what men inherently possess; touch it and it stirs at once. Even among foolish men and simple women, if they hear of a single good deed they will surely all praise it; and however fierce and wicked a man may be, when he sees a good man he dares not offend him. For the arising of the conscience is of itself something that cannot be stopped. That men revere him and say that all men do so must mean that this man’s virtue and Way are truly worthy of reverence, so that there is not one who does not so regard him.

When Sima Wengong set out for the palace, those who saw him laid their hands upon their foreheads, and wherever he went the people blocked the road, saying: “Do not return to Luo, sir; stay and be minister to the Son of Heaven, and keep us common folk alive.” When Liu the Great Remonstrator was at court, there was no one in the world who did not praise his loyalty. When Fu Wenzhong rode his donkey on the Tianjin Bridge, the crowds that followed to look at him emptied the marketplace. Xu Jiexiao kept vigil by his parents’ graves in Huaiyin village, and the people of the city went daily to pay him respect. When Shao Kangjie went out wandering, scholars and commoners alike hurried out with their shoes on backward to welcome him. Such was men’s delight and admiration; the response of Heaven’s intent may be known from it. Had they not truly possessed what deserves reverence, how could they have moved men to such a degree? These several lords, we may say, while alive were ministers and teachers, and after death are spirits and shining ones.

The way of Heaven has no favorites; it is constant in being with the good man. It does not speak, yet subtly responds; it is not summoned, yet comes of itself. If I truly have that whereby to move it, there is nowhere I go that I am not protected. Yet one has only to exhaust one’s own human effort, with a sincere heart that never falters — this is how one comes at last to move Heaven. The Sutra of Rescuing from the Kalpa says: “With the mind thus single, one submits one’s fate to Heaven.” From this we may see that there is not the least thought of courting or hoping.

Master Zhu of the Song said: Heaven and Earth do nothing at all; they take the living of creatures as their mind alone. When a man’s every thought is set on benefiting and succoring, he is himself Heaven and Earth. One who accords with the mind of Heaven — how could Heaven not protect him?

Liu Anshi of the Song submitted a memorial of bold remonstrance distinguishing the upright from the crooked among the court ministers, and further argued that Zhang Dun was a petty man and could not be employed. When Zhang Dun came to power, the duke was banished far away, crossing mountains and putting to sea, driven from place to place without constancy. Men said the duke would surely die, yet in the end he was unharmed. He reached the age of eighty and never once was ill a single day. When the duke was degraded, a certain man, courting Zhang Dun’s favor, asked leave to kill him; and when he galloped to the place where the duke was, about to carry out the deed, he was suddenly struck as if by some thing, and vomited blood and died on the spot.

Tang Ziyu was bringing his father’s coffin home to Jishui from Shu. At that time the autumn floods were at their height and the current in the Qutang Gorge was all the more swift and fierce. When the rain came, the boatmen were greatly frightened. Ziyu wept aloud toward Heaven, and at the first cry of grief the water had already fallen more than twenty zhang. Once they had passed, the water returned to what it had been. Now loyalty and filial piety are the head of all virtues, and therefore the way of Heaven protected him thus. I raise these two cases to stand as examples for the rest. If a man can move Heaven in each matter as it arises, Heaven will surely protect him in each matter as it arises.

The sages and worthies and noble men speak what is good and do what is good, and by their harmonious qi they evoke response, so that auspicious omens naturally accord and answer. The Odes say: “How joyous is the noble man — on him fresh blessings and emoluments descend again.” This is precisely the meaning of “there follows.”

Guo Ziyi of the Tang recovered the two capitals, and his merit overshadowed the Tang imperial house; for twenty years the safety of the realm hung upon his person. His merit-ratings as Director of the Secretariat numbered twenty-four in all. Wealth and honor, long life and great age, children and grandchildren honored and illustrious — such a lot has rarely been matched in any age. Now Lord Guo’s abundance of blessing and richness of emolument came to him because his merit was great and his virtue perfect; it was no lucky accident. Let those who do good take thought of this.

Zheng Zhao of Fengyang in the Ming devoted himself each day to benefiting others. One night he dreamed that he came to the heavenly palace, where he saw the gods set out an empty seat and wait. They said: “You were by nature poor and lowly; because you do good, we have commanded the two gods of blessing and emolument to walk with you. In days to come you shall again occupy this seat.” Zhao awoke, and his good thoughts grew firmer and his fame the more renowned. Where he trod, gold and silver lined his feet; wherever he went, blessing and emolument came paired upon his person. His sons and grandsons were rich and honored and multiplied; he enjoyed emolument and support to the end of his life. In the end he attained liberation from the corpse and was confirmed in the rank of the Perfected of Pure Desire.

Yan Yuan died young in a mean alley; Boyi and Shuqi starved on Mount Shouyang; Yuan Xian was poor; Fan Pang suffered execution — these were men who cultivated virtue yet had little of blessing and emolument. But where good virtue abides, it contends in brightness with the sun and moon and is not to be measured against ordinary blessing and emolument. This is what men who would fulfill benevolence and take up righteousness ought to know.

Evil and uprightness cannot stand together. Where uprightness reaches, evil of itself finds no place — as when the sun comes out, ice and snow melt of themselves. Li Jifu said: The gods love integrity; keep to integrity and the gods receive your offerings. No portent can overcome virtue; when virtue is lost, portents flourish. Such is the natural order of things.

Jing Qing of the Ming, on his way to the metropolitan examination, passed through Chunhua. The daughter of his host was possessed by a specter, and when the lord lodged in that house the specter did not come that night. When Qing left, it returned. The girl asked it why, and it said: “I avoid the scholar Jing.” The girl told her father, and her father pursued Qing; Qing wrote the four words “Jing Qing is here” and bade him paste them on the door, and the specter was stilled. Qing was most loyal and ardent, and to this day he is held in reverence. That which fills and blocks the space between heaven and earth is qi. If the qi suffers no shrinking, then uprightness and greatness flow abroad, and creatures of themselves dare not oppose it. Hence the gentleman has the study of nourishing the qi. To nourish the qi lies in governing the mind: when clarity and brightness dwell in the person and sincerity is kept in calm stability, no creature can hide its true state. But if a man lets his mind grow dim and murky, then there is no need to ask whether evil will come, for this within him has already become a marsh where evil gathers — how could he subdue it at a single encounter?
Gods and men are one in principle. Toward those whom men revere, the gods also extend their protection. As it is said: when a man’s Dao and virtue are weighty, then gods and ghosts alike revere him.

Han Qi of the Song, moving his command from Chengde to Zhongshan, came to Shahe when his outriders suddenly turned back and reported that a violent flood was coming. The lord urgently ordered boats made ready for the crossing. The waves indeed rose like mountains, and the boat was near to capsizing; his followers were greatly terrified. Suddenly a divine dragon dammed the current upstream, and the water at once grew calm. When the crossing was done, the dragon departed, and the water surged and swelled again as before.

Old Master Jin of Yizheng in the Ming kept a pawnshop. At the beginning of the Jiajing era, river pirates plundered the wealthy families almost to the last, yet the Jin household alone came off unharmed. The authorities suspected him of collusion with the robbers, and when the pirates were taken they questioned them as to the reason. The robbers said: “Several times we went to plunder, and were driven off by a god in golden armor.” The official did not believe it and summoned the neighbors and constables to inquire. They all said: “Jin is in truth a man who accumulates virtue. Other pawnshops take in light and give out heavy, but he alone deals fairly both ways; he appraises goods most generously and allows longer terms. Moreover he seeks out the aged and poor and, breaking his own rules, remits their interest; in winter he remits the interest on winter clothing, in summer the interest on summer clothing, and this year after year as a custom. Heaven protects the good man and commands the gods to guard him; what doubt can there be in reason?” The magistrate commended him, memorialized the throne, and had his gate adorned in honor.

Yu Tieqiao said: In speaking before of calamity and evil, the text first said, “All men hate him”; now in speaking of blessing and good, it first says, “All men revere him.” For such matters as the disasters of the evil stars and the protection of the spirits may not be seen at any given moment, whereas that all revere or all hate is the reliable omen that comes first and can be verified. Those who have a mind to learn the Dao should constantly turn back and examine themselves. If many revere me, I know that the spirits’ shielding of me is dense and manifold; if many hate me, I know that the evil star glares directly overhead. The human heart is the will of Heaven; there is no need to seek it in what cannot be seen or heard.

In this world there is no affair that cannot be accomplished, and in all the realm no man who cannot do it. Only do good with a sincere heart, and then human action accords with the heart of Heaven — how should the will of Heaven run counter to man’s wish? Of itself it will aid you in secret, and nothing you do will fail to prosper, nothing you undertake will fail to succeed.

Yu Yubi said: The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching says: “He who indulges this mind destroys man’s good works; gather it to one place, and there is nothing that cannot be done.” It also says: “You bhikshus should be diligent and zealous, and then no task will be hard. It is like a small stream flowing constantly, which can wear through stone. But if the practitioner’s mind is repeatedly slack and idle, it is like drilling for fire and stopping before the wood grows hot: though he wishes to get fire, fire is hard to come by.” The Sutra of the Outcry says: “The wise man smelts his mind with wisdom and searches out every defilement, as iron ore cast into the fire and refined a hundred times becomes pure gold; and as the great ocean, seething day and night, brings forth great treasures. Man is the same: if day and night he taxes his mind without cease, he will attain the fruition of realization.” The Sutra of Forty-Two Sections says: “Now the man who practices the Way is like one man fighting ten thousand: he puts on his armor and goes out from the gate, and his heart may turn cowardly, or he may turn back halfway, or he may die in the struggle, or he may return victorious. A shramana learning the Way should firmly hold his mind, be zealous and keen, fear no circumstance before him, destroy all the maras, and so attain the fruit of the Way.” Patriarch Zhongfeng of Mount Tianmu in the Yuan said: I recall that a Confucian poem exhorting men to learn says, Strike the stone and there is fire; strike it not, and there is no smoke at all. Only when a man learns does he know the Way; without learning it comes not of itself. This says that fire is within the stone, but unless one strikes and draws it out with skill and cunning, one will never meet it. Men today know only that fire is in the stone, yet do not apply the least force of skill to strike it; all day long they point at this cold stone and talk of the uses of fire, talking until their eyes fall to the ground, and it is still a lump of stubborn rock; seek a spark of fire for use, and it is utterly unobtainable. This is the man who will not die to his own will and do the work. There is yet another kind: hearing that fire is in the stone, they smash the stone to bits, wanting to take the fire out, and even grind the stone to dust, yet in the end get no fire; and instead of blaming themselves for not obtaining it by skill, they come to disbelieve that there is truly fire in the stone. This is the ordinary man who does not believe that his own mind can become Buddha. If men today wish to accomplish this matter, they should first take the root of faith as the stone, next take the single raising of the huatou as the hand that strikes the stone, and again take the iron of a firm and irreversible vow to forge a fire-striker; then with the strength of zeal and courage, in the midst of daily activity and stillness, knock at it and strike it without interruption; and again, with the dry grass of the prajñā seed-nature, suddenly bring it about, kindling a single spark that blazes and illumines heaven and earth. This is what is meant by skill and cunning. Master Lianchi of the Ming said: In any single craft or art in the world, at the first learning its difficulty is more than one can bear, and it seems ten thousand times impossible to accomplish; if one then sets it aside and does not learn, in the end there will be no accomplishment. Therefore at the outset what is most precious is a mind of settled resolve free of doubt. Yet though one be resolved, if one is leisurely and slow, then again there is no accomplishment; therefore next what is precious is a mind of zeal and courage. Yet though one be zealous, one may be satisfied with a little gain, or grow weary with long time, or be deluded on meeting favorable circumstance, or fall away on meeting adversity — then again there is no accomplishment; therefore next what is precious is a mind of constancy, firm forever and never turning back. This is what is called a true man of purpose. With the mind thus kept, what affair cannot be accomplished? Should we not strive?

Tai Shang is the ancestor of the Daoist school, and so he speaks wholly of seeking immortality. Mencius said: Every man can become a Yao or a Shun. The Sixth Patriarch of the Chan school in China said: Simply use this mind, and one directly accomplishes Buddhahood. Why did the sages of the three teachings all speak thus, as tally fits with tally? If immortality may be hoped for, Buddhahood attained, and Yao and Shun become, how much more the world’s fame and rank, wealth and honor, long life and sons and daughters? What is there that may be sought and not obtained? It depends only on what the man himself does.

Han Zhongli said: The immortal seeks man far more than man seeks the immortal. Patriarch Lü said: Men often regret that they cannot see me; yet though they saw me every day and could not put my words into practice, what benefit would it be to the matter? From this we may see that man and immortal are one in true nature; it is only that feeling prevails, and so they lose their truth. Once a man returns to the truth and all dusty feelings are exhausted, he is an immortal — how much more if he can aid it with goodness? The Sutra of Embryonic Breathing says: The embryo is formed within the hidden breath, and the breath rests within the embryo. When breath enters the body it is called life; when the spirit departs and leaves the form it is called death. Know that spirit and breath can bring long life: firmly guard emptiness and nothingness to nourish spirit and breath. When the spirit moves, the breath moves; when the spirit abides, the breath abides. If you would have long life, let spirit and breath pour into each other; let the mind stir no thought, neither coming nor going, neither emerging nor entering, and of itself it will abide forever. Practice this diligently, and it is the true road.

Li Duanyuan of the Song asked Chan Master Daguan: “Are heaven and the hells, in the last reckoning, existent or non-existent?” The master said: “The Buddhas speak of the existent within the non-existent, and the eye sees flowers in empty space; the Grand Commandant seeks the non-existent within the existent, and the hand scoops the moon from the water. It is laughable that, seeing a prison before your eyes, you do not flee it, and hearing of heaven beyond the mind, you wish to be born there. You do not know that delight and dread are in the mind, and that good and evil become the realm. Let the Grand Commandant but understand his own mind, and of himself he will be free of confusion.”

Seeking immortality in antiquity: there was Zifang’s loyalty; Wu Meng’s filial piety; Wang Jinxian’s keeping unstained a wife’s chastity; Lan Qi’s brotherly kindness toward his brothers; Liu Yi’s diminishing himself to share with others; Zhao Sutai’s relieving the poor and burying the dead; Xu the Perfected’s dispensing of talismans and distribution of water; Yan Junping’s leading men by goodness; Zhou Bochi’s burying of abandoned bones; Li Wulang’s honesty with the measuring vessel; Chen Anshi’s not killing living beings; Li Xizi’s rescue of starving birds; Yang Jingzhen’s congealing of the spirit in idleness; Tang Ruoshan’s nature free of anger and resentment — even to Huang Wanyou’s few faults, and Jing Xiang’s passionate love of releasing living creatures. Liu Ping’a was originally a physician, Wu Mu a county clerk, Liu Yan a courtesan, Bao Jing a shopkeeper, He Sheng a butcher, Ding Yue a soldier, Zhu a highway robber, Li Zhengyuan a hunter: all these attained immortality through their own accumulation of merit and practice of virtue. Seeking them in the present: Lord Chao Hui is Lord of the Heaven of Quiet Abiding; Lord Zhang Wenqi became the Perfected Lord of Destinies; Lord Wang Su became Vice Minister of the Jade Capital; Lord Lü Hui became the Censor of the Most High; Lord Han Qi presides over the Purple Mansion; Lord Fu Bi administers the Kun Terrace; Lord Wang Sou holds the Iron Wheel of the Auxiliary Sage; Lord Jin San became Protector of the Sage and Count of the Wind; Lord Zhang Xiaoji is Master of Mount Song; Lord Dou Yujun is a Perfected of the Cavern Heavens — even to Lord Ouyang Xiu, who presides over Shenqing, Lord Wang Anguo over Lingzhi, Lord Lü Qin over Qunyu, Lord Shi Yannian over Furong, Lord Chen Jing, who was judge of the Directorate of Rectitude, and Lord Tian Chengjun, master of Weiyang. These too attained immortality through their own accumulation of merit and practice of virtue. As for what the Daoist scriptures record: the second grade of the Middle Prime, the Left Palace of Cavern Yang, and the lands it governs, with the Nine Sovereigns, the Upper Ramparts, the four cardinal points, and the eight extremities — its spirit officials and retainers number in all ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine myriad. All are men who in the world had merit and practice, and who, having received deliverance, were advanced to fill those posts. So too Lord He Xizhi, because he annotated the Diamond Sutra and brought benefit to the world, held after death the office of Examiner of the Calendar and Numbers of the Western Marchmount. Though this is a marchmount bureau, he too is one who received deliverance. These are they who by doing good could hope for immortality. From antiquity to the present, those who became immortals number more than a hundred thousand, and whole households raised to heaven number more than eighty. Therefore it is said: Say not there is no school where immortals may be learned; through all the ages, how many have risen on high! Men today practice without sincerity, and so they say there are no immortals in the world — as though, reciting and following Confucius and Mencius but unable truly to put their teachings into practice, one should therefore say there are no sages and worthies in the world. How could that be right?

The Guide to the Cultivation of Nature and Life says: If you would cultivate long life, you must know the root from which you were born; if you would seek deathlessness, you must understand the deathless one. That deathless one is none other than our own true mind, which fundamentally abides forever. This mind is numinous and undarkened, clearly and constantly aware, neither coming nor going, neither born nor extinguished. Yet the people of the world do not awaken; from beginningless time they have been deluded as to the true mind, and so they undergo the turning wheel and fall vainly into the various destinies. Now the true mind is without delusion; the wisdom of the nature is originally bright, wondrously clear, the primal essence. But when delusion suddenly stirs, in an instant it grows dim, and so that primal essence is lost; clinging to the clear, it gives rise to knowing, and thus wisdom is turned into consciousness. The deluded mind within the body is named consciousness. The mind is originally without knowing; through consciousness it knows. The nature is originally without birth; through consciousness it is born. The seed of the born body sprouts and buds herein, opens the flower of outflows, and bears the fruit of birth and death. Men today vainly suppose that within the square inch there is a thing bright and numinous, undivided and one body with things, and take this to be the primal spirit. They do not know that this is precisely the consciousness-spirit that lives and dies, the seed of the wheel of rebirth through endless kalpas. Therefore it is said: The student of the Way does not know the true, because from the first he takes the consciousness-spirit as his own; the root of birth and death through measureless kalpas, the fool calls the original man. King Yijian asked the Venerable Parati: “What is the Buddha?” He said: “Seeing the nature is the Buddha.” The king said: “Has the master seen the nature?” He said: “I see the Buddha-nature.” The king said: “Where is the nature?” He said: “The nature is in its functioning.” He said: “What is this functioning?” Parati then spoke a verse: In the womb it is the body; in the world, the man. In the eye, it is seeing; in the ear, it is hearing. In the nose, it smells fragrance; in the mouth, it speaks and talks. In the hand, it grasps and holds; in the foot, it runs and races. Everywhere manifest, it embraces the whole dharma-realm; gathered in, it dwells within a single mote of dust. Those who know it know it as the Buddha-nature; those who do not, call it the vital soul. This is why the World-Honored One taught men first to cut off the root of beginningless rebirth. Once this root is cut, the various consciousnesses have nothing to rely on, and we recover our original true and permanent essence — what is called the true, still, wondrously bright, empty, numinous, penetrating, luminous and solitary abiding. Turn from it and one is common; follow it and one is sage. Deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the wheel of rebirth ceases. If you would stop the wheel of rebirth, nothing is better than the twin practice of calm abiding and insight. You must at all times preserve this mean in which the seven emotions have not yet arisen, and in every thought keep whole this essence unstained by the eight consciousnesses. The moment the spirit’s light goes forth, draw it back at once; do not let it shine deludedly for a single instant. An ancient immortal said: The great Dao teaches men first to still their thoughts; if the thoughts are not stilled, all is in vain. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet toward those deluded minds, do not suppress and extinguish them either. Dwelling in the realm of delusive thought, do not add knowing; and in that non-knowing, do not argue what is true and what is false. The Awakening of Faith says: If the mind scatters, gather it in at once and make it abide in right thought. When a thought arises, be aware of it; being aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone. Know that deluded thoughts arise from the root of consciousness, and depending on objects become delusive; they have no real substance. In the time of sentient beings, wisdom is weak and consciousness strong, and so it is merely named consciousness; in the stage of Buddhahood, wisdom is strong and consciousness weak, and so it is merely named wisdom. Only the name is turned, not the substance. The single original source of mind was vast and wondrously clear; because knowing was established upon seeing and knowing, delusive dust arose, and so there are deluded thoughts. If in seeing and knowing there is no seeing, then the nature of wisdom is pure and returns again to the wondrous clarity, and thought and intention dissolve. Once one faculty has returned to its source, the six faculties all become liberation. With no faculties, objects, or six consciousnesses, there is no seed of the wheel of rebirth; the single point of true mind stands alone without support, enduring through ten thousand kalpas, forever without birth or death. This method points directly at the human mind; understand it once and a hundred matters are settled. It is the wondrous secret of becoming Buddha and becoming immortal. If you would seek long life, you must investigate right here.

This section sums up the foregoing, saying that doing good is the road to ascending to the Real. The word ‘to establish’ means to accumulate; the figures a thousand and three hundred fix the number and the term, resolving that it must be accomplished, with no thought of turning back.

Han Zhongli Quan transmitted the elixir to Patriarch Lü Chunyang, the art of turning iron into gold, that he might thereby relieve the world. The Patriarch said: “Will it change in the end?” He said: “After five hundred years it will return to its original substance.” The Patriarch said with a sorrowful look: “If so, then it will harm the men of five hundred years hence; I do not wish to learn it.” Zhongli sighed and said: “To cultivate immortality one must accumulate three thousand deeds and eight hundred merits. This single word of yours has already fulfilled the three thousand and eight hundred.” Again, the Collection of the Ten Thousand Good Deeds All Returning to One says: The ten thousand good deeds are the provisions of the bodhisattva entering the Way; the many practices are the stair and step by which all Buddhas aid the Way. If one has eyes but no feet, how shall one reach the land of coolness? Grasping the real and forgetting the expedient, how shall one ascend to the land of freedom? Therefore true emptiness and wondrous existence ever sustain each other: clouds spread the gate of compassion, waves surge in the sea of practice. From this we see that Buddha and immortal are one thread, and alike come down to teaching men to do good and establish merit; in truth they differ from our Confucianism in name but are the same in substance. Truly, to unite the three in one, one must begin by feeling the pulse and tracing to the source; that they stand as three is because men divide the gates and cling to appearances. Now I urge the people of the world to ponder this principle deeply and give rise to no discrimination: only go and establish merit and do good, and whether you seek Confucianism, Buddha, or immortality, all is within this, with not one failure in ten thousand.

The ancients said: Man’s feelings are like water, and rules and ritual are the dikes. If the dikes are not firm, the water will surely burst forth and rush. If a man’s feelings are not controlled, he will run wild and disorderly without measure. Therefore to put away feeling and still delusion, to forbid evil and stop wickedness, one must not forget the rules for a single breath. It is also said: That a swift horse in its racing dares not let its legs go free is the rein and bit that governs it; that a petty man in his violence dares not give his feelings rein is the punishment of law that restrains him; that the consciousness in its wandering dares not grasp and cling is the work of awareness and illumination. Hence the student who lacks awareness and illumination is like a swift horse without rein or bit, a petty man without law or punishment: how shall he cut off greed and desire, and govern his delusive thoughts?

Suo Jingxu loved learning and did not answer the summons of province or commandery. The governor Yin Dan once paid him a visit and forgot to return for a whole day. Withdrawing, he sighed and said: “The reason the people of the world have a surplus is not that wealth and honor are in their nature; it is that the eye delights in the five colors and the ear toys with sounds. The master casts aside what others gather and gathers what they cast aside. His form dwells amid the dust of the world, but his mind perches in right principle. How could outer things or outer encounters stir his heart?” Now Lord Suo, having seen right principle with thorough mastery, kept to it and followed it as something natural. When men today act against righteousness and turn their backs on principle, and their hearts are stirred and their deeds move — why do they not take this as their model?

This sentence speaks wholly with regard to human affairs. Man’s nature is originally good, yet you take evil as ability: this is to lose the substance of your good nature. In my poor judgment these four words are the root of the sickness of every evildoer, great and small, through a thousand ages; hence they are placed at the head of all evils. However stupid a man may be, there is none who willingly is an evildoer; yet there is also none who does not wish to be an able man. Only because he mistakes the word ‘ability’ does he go on doing worse and worse. At the first he says: The able man is useful, the unable man is useless; the able man makes others fear him, the unable man suffers others’ bullying. In time he himself knows that he does evil, yet he gravely takes his stand as an evildoer and makes no secret of it, and glosses it over with a fair name. The greedy take it as ability to overbear by power and bind by craft and to get much of other men’s wealth, and beautify the name, calling it shrewdness. The fierce take it as ability to be overbearing, cunning, and treacherous, to entrap and harm others, and beautify the name, calling it a ruthless hand. The lewd take it as ability to practice lechery and ply charms, to seduce other men’s wives and daughters, and beautify the name, calling it gallantry. The flatterer takes it as ability to fawn and deceive, and beautifies the name, calling it cleverness. The slanderer takes it as ability to spread rumors and stir up trouble, and beautifies the name, calling it eloquence. Of such kinds there is no end to tell. Vying in splendor and contending in marvel, men make these their fashion; the false sit in them without doubt, and the hearers grow used to them as fine tales. Then if by chance there are one or two men without shrewdness, without a ruthless hand, not gallant, not clever, without eloquence, there is none who does not laugh and point them out as cast-off stuff for the world’s use, rubbish of the times. But when the affair is past and the retribution comes, and the coffin lid is closed and the verdict given — able men have been many; where are they now? Alas! I exhort all men rather to bend for a while and be cast-off stuff and rubbish, and to work for themselves at the final move, being plain yet savoury, steady and never defeated. If you do not believe this, pray look at the world: is there any good man who fails to win Heaven’s protection and men’s reverence, or any evildoer who escapes Heaven’s punishment and men’s hatred?

The Buddha said: All the evildoers in the world fall into the hells when they die. The hells have a warden, Ox-Head A-pang, whose nature is fierce and evil, with not one thought of kindness or forbearance. Seeing all sentient beings receive this evil retribution, he grieves only that they are not more miserable, only that they are not more cruelly tormented. Someone asked the hell-warden: “The sufferings of sentient beings are deeply to be pitied; yet you always harbor cruelty and poison, with no heart of compassion.” The hell-warden answered: “Those who come to suffer these sufferings for such evil deeds are all men who were unfilial to father and mother, who slandered the Three Treasures, who reviled the six relations, who slighted and insulted teachers and elders, who framed the good and innocent, who killed living beings, who created every manner of evil karma. When such men come here to suffer, at every point when they are about to be released to birth I always exhort them, saying: The extremes of suffering here cannot be endured; now that you have got out, do no more evil. Yet these sinners do not repent at all; released today, in a moment they return, turning and turning through the wheel of rebirth, and they do not know their pain. For this reason I have not one heart of compassion toward sinners.” Know therefore that the man who does evil will surely fall into the hells. As it is now, since you have obtained a moment’s abiding in the world, you should at once strive to practice kindness and compassion, broadly cultivate all good deeds, dissolve the three obstructions, purify the six faculties, recite the Buddha’s name and keep the fasts, practice Chan meditation and learn the Way, rise above the three realms, and escape utterly the four modes of birth. Never give rein to greed, anger, and delusion, nor do deeds of killing, theft, and lust, creating such evil karma and receiving such evil fruit. The Buddha’s word is not false; men should firmly believe.

Yu Sixuan of the Tang was exceedingly ingenious by nature. Empress Wu wished to make the petition-box by which men might secretly accuse one another of hidden matters; no craftsman could make it, but Sixuan made it, and it greatly pleased her will. Someone cast a petition into the box accusing Sixuan of having made for Xu Jingye at Yangzhou a blade-wheel with which to charge the ranks, killing and wounding a great many government troops. He was accordingly put to death.

Xu Jingye of the Tang raised troops, and Empress Wu was troubled by him. She wished to set up a great case of treason and remove those who opposed her. Suo Yuanli, divining her intent, at once sent up a memorial speaking of an urgent emergency; he was summoned to audience, promoted to General of the Roaming Cavalry and made an examining commissioner, and at the office of the governor of Luozhou he established a special tribunal. He kept several hundred ruffians; when he meant to ruin someone, he had several places accuse him at once, with statements all identical. Once in prison, the man was threatened with savage torture, and none failed to confess falsely. From one prisoner he would trace out the whole root and stem, implicating as many as several hundreds. Afterward, because he took bribes, he was arrested and handed over to the subordinate officials. He would not confess, and the official said: “Bring the lord’s iron cage.” Yuanli submitted to the charge and died in prison. At the same time there was Zhou Xing, cruel by nature and banded with Suo Yuanli and his like. Someone accused Xing of plotting treason; the Empress Dowager was angry and commanded Lai Junchen to interrogate him. Junchen and Xing were then jointly trying cases, and he said to Xing: “Many prisoners will not confess — what is to be done?” Xing said: “Easy enough. Fetch a great jar and heat it on all sides with charcoal fire, and make the prisoner enter it — what will he not confess?” Junchen then had a great jar and charcoal fire brought, exactly as Xing had described, and said to Xing: “I have received an order from within to try you, elder brother; pray enter this jar.” Xing trembled and confessed his crime, and was exiled to Lingnan, where he was killed in a quarrel among his enemies.

In the time of Emperor Huizong of the Song, Song Sheng, at the beginning of the Zhenghe era, was transport commissioner of Jingxi and was charged with building the Western Inner Palace. He once said: “Finish this task quickly, and the reward may be had at once.” He used ox-bone mixed with lime, and when that ran short he dug up human bones from the pauper’s burying ground and burned them to ash in its place. Sun Kuang, the assistant transport commissioner, tried to stop him, but he would not listen; pleading illness, Sun resigned and left. Sheng, for his merit, was appointed a Scholar and summoned to the post of Director of the Palace Administration. He suddenly contracted a foul disease, and said himself that for the evil of burning bones his crime deserved the extinction of his family; he vomited blood and died. Before long the whole household died. Later Sun Kuang died of illness and came to the underworld, where he saw Song Sheng on an iron bed and copper pillar, blood streaming over his whole body. He came to a hall where the underworld official said to him: “You admonished him and he would not listen, and you gave up your office and went home — you are truly a man with a human heart; your life should be extended by twelve years.” And so he was given life again, and told men of the matter. Now the most miserable thing under heaven is nothing like the overthrow of one’s ancestral line and the extinction of one’s clan. Sheng, for a single thought of coveting reward, met with this suffering. The ancients said: Evil arises from greed, and greed is the root of evil; the way to cure evil begins with removing greed. How true! As for the other paths by which men take evil for ability, they cannot be fully enumerated, nor could one bear to record them all. Let men examine themselves according to the matter at hand.

The Zhongjie Sutra says: If a man commits one evil, his mind is not at peace; for ten evils, his strength is weak and thin; for twenty evils, he meets with obstruction and decline, and all his affairs go contrary; for fifty evils, he never finds a spouse; up to a hundred evils, water and fire become his calamities, and he is dragged into trouble without cause and dies a bad death under the law; for five hundred evils, his sons and grandsons are cut off; for a thousand evils, traitors and rebellious sons come forth from his house, his clan is exterminated, and his descendants generation after generation take strange forms and changed bodies and enter among the birds and beasts. When evil is accumulated to the full, disaster reaches later generations, and that he himself should enter the hells is the lighter part of it. Men should take this instruction and hold it in mind at every moment; then of themselves they will do no evil.

This sentence speaks wholly with regard to the lives of living creatures. The great virtue is called giving life; yet you harden your heart to do maiming and harm. Now to maim, wound, poison, and injure is the greatest of evils; and when it comes moreover from a hardened heart, then wherever the will turns there is not the least particle of compassion or pity. All good is rooted in one kindness; all evil is rooted in one hardness of heart. To put away hardness and be kind — herein lies the achievement of sages and worthies, Buddhas and immortals.

To covet life and dread death, to love kin and cling to the familiar, to know pain and feel suffering — in these, creatures and men are the same. It is only that man has intelligence and creatures have none, that man can speak and creatures cannot, that man’s strength is great and creatures’ strength is weak. When men today prepare a single dish, they do not kill only one creature. For doves, pigeons, quails, and sparrows, more than ten lives are taken to make one broth; for clams, mussels, shrimp, and cockles, a single broth takes more than a hundred lives. And there are those who love fine flavors and seek their own ease, who have delicacies brought from afar, or keep creatures ready and wait to cook them, or pickle live crabs in the lees, or keep fish and make minced fish, or gather charcoal to roast alive, or pierce for blood and swallow raw, or open the belly to take the embryo, or strip the skin and scoop out the shell — a hundred schemes of boiling and frying, a thousand ways of dressing and making. When they have eaten their fill they are puffed with complacency; if it is a little late they rage and curse the cook. Think deeply, ponder painfully: truly this is cause for dismay and grief. The scripture says: All things fear the knife and the rod, and there are none that do not love their lives. Therefore Wang Ke killed a sheep, and the sheep ran to a guest and bowed to plead; Zou Sheng cut open a deer, and the deer knelt and wept and swallowed its voice. A startled bird flew to the table and begged its life of Lord Wei; a hunted beast entered a hut and sought life from Master Ou. So too the Hanlin Academician Shen, when he was assistant prefect of Jiangning, killed sheep in his kitchen, and again and again the knife went missing; peering in, he saw a sheep carrying the knife in its mouth and hiding it beneath the wall. Yang Jie, when he was judicial commissioner, was wandering on Mount Ayuwang and fell asleep at noon, dreaming of more than a hundred women who seemed to be pleading something; secretly he looked into the traveling kitchen, and knew that it was the clams seeking life. Now if living creatures’ love and attachment is like this, how much more when they are seized, with no place to flee death, looking at their kind beside them and unable to cling to them, crying out in grief as they go to execution, bearing their sorrow to the end; and when they have suffered butchering and cutting, they enter the cauldron and the tripod — every kind of pain piercing to the marrow of the bone. At such a time, in such a state, how are they different from men? When men today suffer the least hurt from hot water, fire, knife, or needle, they cry out and beg for rescue; a moment’s dizziness or eye-pain, and they call the doctor and buy medicine. They cherish their own bodies so; why is it that toward creatures alone they do not give rise to pity, but maim and harm at will, binding up enmity and creating karma? Alas, alas! Among all evils, this is the most pitiable. Buddhas and immortals warn and exhort, and the way of Heaven loves to return what is given. You should urgently put yourself in their place and at once awaken with a start. Therefore the various items on which slaughter is not permitted are set out in full below, and I humbly beg men of benevolence and noble character to follow and practice them.

The day of one’s birth is called the mother’s ordeal. While one’s parents live, one ought surely to purify the heart and show reverence; when they are dead, one should all the more eat vegetarian food and cry out to Heaven. How then can one indulge the mouth and belly by killing living creatures? Therefore on one’s birthday one must not take life.

All men grieve when they have no son and rejoice when they have one. Now you celebrate your own son’s birth by causing another’s son to die. Moreover, when an infant is newly born, should one not seek long life for it, instead of creating karma? Therefore on the birth of a son one must not take life.
